# PropGen: Automated Property Generation for Property-Based Testing of Mobile Apps

- Authors: Xiong, Yiheng; Song, Shiwen; Ma, Bo; Su, Ting; Xie, Xiaofei
- Year / venue: 2026, Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (published)
- DOI: 10.1145/3832783.3837536 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3832783.3837536
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index). The PDF is arXiv v2 (8 Oct 2026) carrying the ASE '26 camera-ready header and DOI (p. 1); peer-reviewed (received 2026-03-26, accepted 2026-06-18, p. 13).

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
- [A] Automate the construction of properties for property-based testing (PBT) of mobile apps with LLMs. A *property* here is a rule of the form precondition -> interaction -> expected postcondition that must hold whenever it applies; PBT then generates many GUI event sequences and checks whether the rule is violated (p. 1, p. 3).
- [A] Motivation: non-crashing functional bugs lack explicit test oracles; PBT can expose them, but writing properties by hand is "difficult and expensive", and apps rarely have specifications (p. 1). Asking an LLM directly for properties is unreliable because, without evidence of how the app behaves, "LLMs tend to hallucinate properties that the app never satisfies" (p. 2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [V] RQ1: effectiveness in exploring app functionalities and generating valid properties; RQ2: how often properties are imprecise (cause false positives) and how well refinement fixes them; RQ3: whether generated properties find new functional bugs; RQ4: comparison with prior functional-testing techniques in finding new bugs (p. 6).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Tool design plus empirical evaluation on 12 Android apps, with human annotation of validity, comparison against baselines, and bug reporting to developers (p. 6-8).
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] PropGen has three stages (p. 3-6): (1) **hypothesis-guided exploration**: an MLLM looks at the screenshot (with numbered widgets from the accessibility tree), app name and the activity names extracted from the AndroidManifest.xml file (p. 4), and proposes candidate functionalities each tied to a triggering widget; PropGen executes them step by step, the MLLM labels each step success/fail/complete, and traces are summarised into "behavioral evidence" (state before, event, state after, state diff, outcome); random exploration is used when no unexplored hypothesis remains (p. 4-5); widget signatures keep only app-defined text, filtered against "a whitelist extracted via static analysis" (p. 5); (2) **property synthesis**: the MLLM first writes a natural-language property (precondition P, interaction I, postcondition Q) from the evidence, then translates it into executable code for the PBT tool Kea (p. 6); (3) **feedback-driven refinement**: for properties whose reported violations are *manually confirmed* false positives, the LLM locates which of P, I or Q is imprecise using the source trace and the failing run, and edits only that part (p. 4, p. 6).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] RQ1: DroidAgent (LLM-based functionality exploration) and a naive LLM baseline that writes 20 properties per app from the app's official description without running the app (p. 7). RQ4: Genie, Odin (automated differential oracles), PBFDroid (PBT for data-manipulation functionalities) and VisionDroid (LLM multi-agent functional bug detection) (p. 7).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] 12 popular open-source Android apps (e.g. OmniNotes, Markor, AnkiDroid, NewPipe), 57,529 to 403,785 LOC; GitHub stars 1.1K-37.5K (p. 7).
- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 12 apps. Units of analysis: 1,282 functionalities inferred by PropGen (575 by DroidAgent), 985 generated properties, 240 naive-baseline properties, 127 imprecise properties, 25 new bugs (p. 8-10).
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Eight apps adopted from prior functional-bug studies, excluding apps no longer runnable/maintained or functionally similar to already chosen ones; four more popular open-source Google Play apps added "to further improve diversity" (p. 6-7). [I] No power or sample-size reasoning reported.
- Data availability (public? link?): [A] "We have made all the artifacts publicly available" (p. 11), Zenodo artifact doi:10.5281/zenodo.21770804 (p. 13). Not checked by us.

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Ubuntu 22.04, 192 CPU cores (AMD EPYC 9654), official Android 11 Pixel emulators; GPT-5.2 (snapshot gpt-5.2-2025-12-11) as backend MLLM for PropGen and DroidAgent with default decoding (temperature 1.0, top-p 1.0); 3 h per app for evidence construction and property synthesis, then 6 h of Kea PBT per app (p. 7). Built on DroidBot, uiautomator2 and ADB; mainly Python and JavaScript (p. 6). RQ4 time budgets aligned: 9 h per app for Genie, Odin and VisionDroid; 6 h testing for PBFDroid after the authors manually wrote its DMF properties (p. 8). [I] DroidAgent's time budget is not stated explicitly (not reported).
- Human annotation: [V] two graduate students in software engineering (each at least four years of Android experience), not co-authors, labelled independently; Cohen's kappa 0.91 (functionality validity), 0.82 (execution correctness), 0.81 (property validity); disagreements then resolved by discussion (p. 7).
- Code availability: [A] artifacts released on Zenodo (p. 11, p. 13).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
  - [V] **Functionality validity**: share of inferred functionalities that really exist in the app (human judged from screenshot) (p. 7).
  - [V] **Execution correctness**: share of inferred functionalities whose executed event sequence actually realises them (human judged) (p. 7).
  - [V] **Property validity**: property is valid only if every referenced widget/event appears in its source trace (automated groundedness check) and annotators judge P, I and Q faithful to the intended functionality (p. 7). Chosen because "mobile apps lack ground-truth specifications" (p. 7). Validity does not imply precision (p. 7).
  - [V] **Refinement success**: revised property must (a) still hold on its source trace, (b) no longer raise the spurious violation, and (c) be confirmed valid and intent-preserving by humans (p. 8).
  - [V] **New bugs**: manually confirmed, previously unreported functional bugs, reported to developers (p. 8); for RQ4 also a manual **scope analysis** of whether each prior tool's oracle could in principle detect each bug, partly validated by consulting authors of Genie, Odin and PBFDroid (p. 8). [I] These tools share authors with PropGen (see §9).
  - [V] **Cost**: tokens and USD per LLM call and per app (p. 9).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [I] None found; results are counts and percentages with no repeated runs reported (checked pp. 7-10). The paper states "This single run" only for the RQ4 prior techniques (p. 8). [V] Only inter-rater agreement (Cohen's kappa) is reported (p. 7).

## 7. Key findings
1. PropGen inferred 1,282 functionalities, 1,210 valid (94.4%) and 977 correctly executed (76.2%), vs DroidAgent 575 inferred, 491 valid (85.4%), 187 correctly executed (32.5%) — [V] (p. 8, p. 9).
2. PropGen generated 985 properties, 912 valid (92.6%; 78.7%-98.8% per app) — [V] (p. 8). The naive LLM baseline (app description only) produced 240 properties, none valid, because it referenced non-existent widgets — [V] (p. 9).
3. 127 properties caused false positives during PBT; 118 (92.9%) were successfully refined, mostly by changing the postcondition (64) or precondition (53), only 1 by changing the interaction; of 9 failures, 5 were misdiagnoses and 4 drifted from the original intent — [V] (p. 9).
4. Properties found 25 previously unknown functional bugs in the latest app versions; 5 fixed by developers at writing time; categories: functionality does not take effect (12), state inconsistency (6), unexpected wrong behaviour (4), navigation failure (3) — [V] (p. 9-10).
5. Of the 25 bugs, only 7 (28%) were in the detection scope of the four prior tools and 3 (12%) were rediscovered; the prior tools together found 13 unknown bugs, of which PropGen missed 10 — [V] (p. 10). [A] The approaches are "complementary rather than substitutable" (p. 10).
6. Cost: about $14.86 and 6,364k tokens per app for PropGen vs $13.01 and 5,109k tokens for DroidAgent; refinement about $0.02 per property — [V] (p. 9).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Manual inspection of functionalities and properties may introduce subjectivity and bias; mitigated by two independent annotators and consensus (p. 11).
- [A] The 12 apps may not represent the diversity of real-world apps; a larger and broader set is planned (p. 11).
- [A] Open-source apps may be in GPT-5.2's training data; mitigated by checking that none of the 25 bugs was previously reported, and by noting that six of the 12 tested builds were released after the model's training cutoff and still yielded bugs (p. 11).
- [A] Failure modes: the MLLM sometimes proposes non-existent functionalities, executions may not finish within the step budget or are labelled successful too early, and synthesis occasionally hallucinates widgets despite grounding (p. 9). PropGen generates only one property per functionality and lacks the differential oracles of Genie/Odin (p. 10).
- [A] A pre-existing app fault could in principle corrupt generated or refined properties; risk argued to be limited because properties come only from successful traces and refinements are human-confirmed (p. 10-11).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] **Not fully automatic.** Refinement is triggered only after a human confirms a violation is a false positive (p. 4, p. 6), and bug confirmation is manual (p. 8). The cost of this human effort is not reported.
- [I] **No repeated runs with temperature 1.0.** A single run is stated for the RQ4 prior techniques (p. 8). For PropGen's RQ1-RQ3 no repetition is reported. Decoding is stochastic (p. 7), so it is unknown how stable the counts are.
- [I] **Weak naive baseline.** The naive baseline sees only the app's description, never the GUI (p. 7). Its 0/240 result shows that runtime evidence is needed, but does not test simpler runtime-grounded alternatives.
- [I] **Author-tool overlap.** Ting Su (PropGen co-author) co-authored Genie, Odin, PBFDroid, Kea and Kea2. Xiong co-authored Genie, Kea and Kea2, and Bo Ma co-authored Kea2 (refs [29], [51], [52], [63], [71], p. 12-13). So three of the four RQ4 baselines (Genie, Odin, PBFDroid, p. 7) come from the PropGen authors' own group. The scope analysis is manual (p. 8). Its validation by "the authors of Genie, Odin, and PBFDroid" (p. 8) involves the same group. The PBFDroid properties were written by the PropGen authors (p. 8). Only VisionDroid (p. 7) is independent. This is not necessarily bias in PropGen's favour, since the group knows these tools well. But the scope analysis is not independently validated.
- [I] **Annotator blinding and kappa scope not reported.** Whether the annotators were blind to which tool (PropGen or DroidAgent) produced each functionality is not reported (p. 7). The set of items over which Cohen's kappa was computed (PropGen only, or both tools) is not stated (p. 7).
- [I] **Contamination check is partial.** "Not previously reported" bugs (p. 11) do not show that the model lacks prior knowledge of app behaviour; app functionality, not bugs, is what the model may have memorised.
- [I] **Validity is judged against human understanding, not a specification** (p. 7). This is reasonable but means "valid" depends on annotators' familiarisation of at least fifteen minutes per app (p. 7).

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Same MLLM backend for PropGen and DroidAgent (p. 7) is a fair control. Budget alignment across tools in RQ4 (p. 8) is reasonable, but tools differ in design scope, which the authors address with the scope analysis (p. 8). Possible training-data exposure of open-source apps (p. 11).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] 12 open-source Android apps on emulators (p. 7); unclear transfer to iOS, web, closed-source or login/network-heavy apps.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] "Valid" properties are grounded and faithful but may still be imprecise (p. 7); bug counts depend on each tool's oracle type, which the authors acknowledge ("Raw bug counts alone are therefore not directly comparable", p. 8).
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No statistical tests; 12 apps; no repeated runs reported (single run stated for RQ4 baselines, p. 8). High kappa values (0.81-0.91, p. 7) support annotation reliability.
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [I] Good: model snapshot, decoding parameters, budgets, hardware and artifacts are reported (p. 7, p. 13). Proprietary model dependence and temperature 1.0 limit exact replication.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A] (p. 9-11): evaluate on a larger and broader set of apps (p. 11); interact-then-infer functionality inference, activity transition graphs for step planning, explicit completion checks, post-synthesis widget checks (p. 9); richer context and an intent-verification step for refinement (p. 9); more properties per functionality and combining PropGen with specialised oracles (p. 10).
- Suggested by us [I]: use properties mined from an original app as a behavioural oracle for an AI-reconstructed version of that app (differential fidelity testing), and measure how many original-app properties the rebuild satisfies.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2, RQ4, RQ5 (indirect); RQ1 only tangentially. Not RQ3.
- How it informs our work [I]: PropGen does not generate or reconstruct applications, so it gives no direct evidence on fidelity or code quality of AI-built apps. Its value is as a method. It recovers behavioural specifications from a running app without source code or written specifications. It does this through runtime observation plus light static analysis of the APK: manifest activity names (p. 4) and a string whitelist (p. 5). So it is grey-box rather than purely observational. The authors call this "exploring a black-box app" [A] (p. 11). This is exactly the kind of oracle a reverse-engineering study needs to check functional fidelity (RQ2, RQ5). Its result that an LLM without runtime observation produces 0 valid properties (p. 9) supports grounding any reconstruction or test generation in observed behaviour. Its evaluation design (independent annotators with kappa, scope analysis for oracle-dependent tools) is a good template for RQ4. Relevance is therefore medium.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ2 | Behavioural properties can be recovered from a running Android app without source or specs (runtime observation plus manifest activity names and a static string whitelist): 912 of 985 LLM-generated properties judged valid (92.6%) | 4, 5, 8, 9 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | An LLM given only the app description produced 240 properties, none valid (hallucinated widgets); runtime evidence is required | 9 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Generated properties found 25 previously unknown functional bugs in 12 apps; prior tools rediscovered 3 of them, but themselves found 13 unknown bugs, 10 of which PropGen missed; authors call the approaches complementary (A) | 9, 10 | V | moderate |
| RQ4 | Validity judged by 2 independent non-author annotators (kappa 0.91 / 0.82 / 0.81); no ground-truth spec exists for apps | 7 | V | moderate |
| RQ4 | Bug counts across functional-testing tools are oracle-dependent and not directly comparable; scope analysis used instead | 8, 10 | V | moderate |
| RQ4 | No repeated runs reported (single run stated for RQ4 baselines) at temperature 1.0; no variance or statistical tests found (our check) | 7, 8 | I | moderate |
| RQ5 | Imprecise LLM properties are common (127 of 985 caused false positives) but 92.9% could be refined, mainly via pre/postconditions | 9 | V | moderate |

Strength note [I]: moderate = peer-reviewed (ASE 2026) single study with 12 apps and good annotation reliability, but no replication or variance.

## 14. Key quotes
> "none of which is valid" (p. 9)

> "Raw bug counts alone are therefore not directly comparable across" (p. 8)

> "Neither annotator is a co-author" (p. 7)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: sections read / skipped and why: all 13 PDF pages read via `fulltext.txt` (abstract to conclusion, data availability, acknowledgements); reference list (p. 12-13) skimmed for author overlap only. Figures 1-2 (p. 3) are diagrams whose content is described in the text. The two-column layout interleaves lines in `fulltext.txt`; all numbers were taken from tables and checked against the text.
- Uncertainties: (1) DroidAgent's exploration time budget in RQ1 is not stated explicitly; (2) the human effort for confirming false positives and bugs is not quantified; (3) the abstract in metadata.json is truncated, but the full text was available; (4) the 25 bugs' report links/IDs on public trackers are not given in the paper (Table 4 lists IDs 1-25 internal to the paper, p. 10).
- Critical-review fixes X1-X5 of `reports/critical-review-batch-c.md` applied 2026-11-12 after checking pp. 4-5, 7, 8, 10, 11 and 12-13.
- Funding [V]: National Research Foundation Singapore / CyberSG R&D Programme Office and NSFC projects (p. 11). [I] We found no conflict-of-interest statement beyond this.

# Is LLM-Generated Code More Maintainable & Reliable Than Human-Written Code?

- Authors: Molison, Alfred Santa; Moraes, Marcia; Melo, Glaucia; Santos, Fabio; Assunção, Wesley K. G.
- Year / venue: 2025, 2025 ACM/IEEE International Symposium on Empirical Software Engineering and Measurement (ESEM) (published)
- DOI: 10.1109/esem64174.2025.00036 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1109/esem64174.2025.00036
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index). The PDF analysed is the arXiv version, "arXiv:2508.00700v1 [cs.SE] 1 Aug 2025" (p. 1), from arxiv.org/pdf/2508.00700; page numbers refer to our PDF, not the ESEM proceedings pagination.

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
- [A] Compare internal quality attributes (maintainability and reliability) of LLM-generated and human-written Python code, including the SonarQube-estimated effort to fix issues, across three task difficulty levels and three LLM configurations (zero-shot, few-shot, fine-tuning) (p. 1).
- [A] Secondary aim: provide a reusable experimentation infrastructure (LLM + PostgreSQL + SonarQube) for replications and automated quality analysis (p. 1).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [V] Single RQ: "Is LLM-Generated Code More Maintainable and Reliable than Human-Written Code?" (p. 1).
- [V] The only explicit null hypothesis is H0 of equal effort-in-minutes distributions between groups (p. 7, p. 9). No hypotheses are stated for bugs or code smells; these are compared with odds ratios (p. 6).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Quantitative comparative study (static analysis of four solution sets) plus a small manual functional-correctness check (Pass@1) and qualitative inspection of failures (p. 3, p. 5, p. 8).
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] GPT-4o-2024-08-06 via the OpenAI API, used in three configurations: zero-shot prompt, few-shot prompt, and a fine-tuned GPT-4o (p. 4). The authors call all three "prompt engineering techniques" (p. 4).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Human solutions from the APPS dataset serve as the baseline ("the human dataset") (p. 4). Pairwise comparisons: each LLM configuration vs human, few-shot vs zero-shot, fine-tuned vs zero-shot (p. 6, p. 8). Few-shot vs fine-tuned is not reported.

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] APPS dataset (Hendrycks et al., NeurIPS 2021): 10,000 Python coding questions with multiple human solutions per question, labelled introductory, interview or competition (p. 3, p. 11). Human solutions were collected from Codeforces, AtCoder, Kattis and Codewars and curated by students over six months (p. 3–4).
- Sample size (N) and unit:
  - [V] Fine-tuning: 80 random questions per level for training (240 total); 160 questions per level for testing (480 total) (p. 4).
  - Number of questions submitted for zero-shot and few-shot generation: not reported (the text says "each coding question" was submitted, p. 4, but does not say whether this means all 10,000 or the 480 test questions).
  - Number of human solutions analysed by SonarQube: not reported. APPS has several human solutions per question (p. 3); whether all, one, or a sample were used is not stated.
  - [V] Twelve SonarQube result files (4 datasets × 3 difficulty levels) (p. 5).
  - [V] Pass@1 evaluated on 15 solutions per approach, 5 per difficulty level (p. 7–8).
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Fine-tuning training questions were drawn at random (p. 4). [A] The performance sample was "randomized" and "representative" (p. 10). Whether the 480 test questions were disjoint from the 240 training questions: not reported.
- Data availability (public? link?): [V] APPS is public; replication package on Zenodo (record 15283737) (p. 1, p. 11).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
  - [V] Model GPT-4o-2024-08-06, chosen as the latest model that allowed fine-tuning; temperature 1.00, max tokens 2048, top-p 1.00, frequency and presence penalties 0.00 (p. 4).
  - [V] Zero-shot prompt: "Generate a Python code (only one solution) to solve this question:" plus the problem text (p. 4).
  - [V] Few-shot prompt: the question followed by all human solutions for that same question from APPS ("Sample Solution {index}" entries) (p. 4).
  - [V] Fine-tuning: GPT base model trained on 240 question–answer pairs; training loss 0.21; 496,176 tokens (p. 4). Epochs and other fine-tuning hyper-parameters not reported.
  - Number of generations per question: not reported (one solution per prompt is implied by the zero-shot prompt wording, p. 4). Repeated runs or seeds: not reported.
  - [V] SonarQube Free Server edition, default Python quality profile and quality gate; a new SonarQube project is created before each scan so that all files count as new code; scans driven by Python scripts via SonarScanner CLI; results stored in PostgreSQL (p. 4–5).
  - SonarQube version: the docs link points to SonarQube Server 10.8 (p. 4); exact installed version not otherwise reported.
  - [V] Infrastructure: Ubuntu Linux VM in a VPC with SonarQube, Grafana, PostgreSQL and Python (p. 3).
  - [V] Pass@1: three authors ran sampled solutions with `python3 file.py`, fed inputs from the test cases in the problem description, and checked outputs (p. 5, p. 8).
- Code availability: [V] Scripts and replication package available on Zenodo (p. 3, p. 11).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
  - [V] SonarQube Bugs (reliability: coding errors causing runtime failures or unexpected behaviour), Vulnerabilities (security), Code Smells (maintainability) (p. 5).
  - [V] Severity levels Blocker, Critical, Major, Minor (p. 5).
  - [V] Effort-in-minutes: SonarQube's estimated time to fix issues (p. 5).
  - [V] Normalised issue percentage per dataset ("proportion of rows") (p. 5–6).
  - [V] Pass@1 (Chen et al. formula), k = 1 (p. 5).
  - [A] Metrics were chosen because prior studies used reliability, maintainability and security, and SonarQube is a standard static-analysis tool (p. 2–3).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals):
  - [V] Effort: Mann-Whitney U test with Cliff's delta, Romano et al. thresholds (negligible < 0.147, small < 0.33, medium < 0.474, else large) (p. 5).
  - [V] Bugs and code smells: odds ratios from 2×2 contingency tables per comparison, with significance stars (p. 5–6, p. 8). The test that produced the p-values for the odds ratios is not named.
  - Confidence intervals: not reported. Correction for multiple comparisons: not reported (15 comparisons per table across Tables II–IV, p. 8). Power analysis: not reported.

## 7. Key findings
1. [V] SonarQube found no security vulnerabilities in any dataset (p. 5).
2. [V] Odds of a SonarQube bug in LLM solutions vs human solutions were very low in every configuration and level: zero-shot 0.008 / 0.006 / 0.0005, few-shot 0.003 / 0.006 / 0.001, fine-tuned 0.00 / 0.019 / 0.0005 (introductory / interview / competition), all p < 0.001 (Table II, p. 8).
3. [V] Code smells were mixed: zero-shot had 3.57× the odds of a smell vs human for introductory problems (p < 0.001); few-shot vs human was 0.52 for competition (p < 0.05); fine-tuned vs human was 0.00 for introductory and competition (p < 0.001); several other comparisons were not significant (Table III, p. 8).
4. [V] In the human dataset, bug-type issues were dominated by Blocker severity (87.50% introductory, 71.27% interview, 86.30% competition, Table I) (p. 8). [A] The authors interpret these as "bug rates" (p. 6).
5. [V] Average SonarQube effort to fix (min): introductory human 7.20, zero-shot 3.75, few-shot 4.72, fine-tuned 5.00; interview human 7.06, zero-shot 5.48, few-shot 6.13, fine-tuned 4.67; competition human 6.95, zero-shot 6.14, few-shot 7.33, fine-tuned 7.60 (Fig. 6, p. 7). [A] "LLMs reduced effort in simpler tasks, but this advantage diminished as the tasks became more complex" (p. 7).
6. [V] Cliff's delta for effort, zero-shot vs human: 0.54 large (introductory), 0.21 small (interview), 0.1 negligible (competition), all significant; fine-tuned vs human introductory 0.24 small and fine-tuned vs zero-shot introductory −0.50 large are not marked significant (Table IV, p. 8).
7. [V] Severity shift: for interview problems fine-tuning had 94.1% minor, 2.1% major, 1.2% critical, 2.6% blocker issues, vs human 10.7% blocker (p. 6). For competition problems the human dataset had the fewest critical issues relative to LLM outputs (p. 6). [A] LLMs "may introduce more critical issues compared to human-generated code" on competition tasks (Finding 3, p. 6).
8. [V] Pass@1 on 15 sampled solutions per approach: human 1.0, zero-shot 0.53, few-shot 0.87, fine-tuned 0.47 (Table V, p. 8). Partial (some test cases passed) solutions: 47% of zero-shot, 13% of few-shot and fine-tuned (p. 8). Failures included runtime errors, wrong outputs, hard-coded inputs, waiting for input indefinitely and syntax errors (p. 8).
9. [A] The fine-tuned model has "the best quality metrics" yet "struggled to generate code for complex solutions" (p. 8); the authors attribute its low performance to too few fine-tuning samples (p. 9).
10. [A] AI models "may better avoid functional bugs than address structural code quality concerns" (p. 9).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Possible cross-contamination of coding patterns or prompts between instances, affecting comparisons across zero-shot, few-shot and fine-tuned conditions (p. 10).
- [A] Prompt sensitivity: different wording could give significantly different results (p. 10).
- [A] Python only and competitive-programming style problems; limited generalisability to other languages and real-world software development (p. 10).
- [A] Only GPT-4 (GPT-4o) and a fine-tuned version; may not represent other LLMs (p. 10).
- [A] APPS lacks contextual information about the human-written code (p. 10).
- [A] Performance sample may not represent the population (p. 10).
- [A] LLM parameter and token-limit variations were not tested (p. 10).
- [A] SonarQube metrics may not capture all aspects of quality; its effort estimates may not reflect real developer effort (p. 10).
- [A] Fine-tuning used a limited number of rows due to resource constraints (p. 10).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] Few-shot leakage: the few-shot prompt contains the human reference solutions to the same question (p. 4). Few-shot outputs can therefore copy or adapt the baseline itself, so few-shot vs human is not an independent comparison and the high few-shot Pass@1 (0.87, p. 8) may partly reflect this. Based on the prompt description, p. 4.
- [I] Quality and correctness are not linked: static-quality comparisons include LLM solutions that fail the tests (fine-tuned Pass@1 0.47, p. 8). "Fewer bugs" in SonarQube terms is not "more correct" code. The headline "LLM-generated code has fewer bugs" (p. 1) uses SonarQube's rule-based "bug" category, not functional failures. Based on p. 5 and p. 8.
- [I] Unit of analysis and denominators unclear: the number of human solutions and of zero-/few-shot solutions analysed is not reported (p. 3–4), and normalised percentages are described as "proportion of rows" (p. 5) without defining a row. Odds ratios therefore cannot be reconstructed from the paper.
- [I] Baseline quality: APPS human solutions are competitive-programming submissions written for correctness, not maintainability, as the authors themselves note (p. 9). They are a weak and possibly unfair baseline for maintainability claims.
- [I] Data contamination: APPS has been public since 2021 (p. 11), so GPT-4o may have seen its problems and solutions in training. The paper does not discuss this; its "cross-contamination" limitation (p. 10) concerns prompts, not training data.
- [I] Single sample per question at temperature 1.0 (p. 4), with no repeated runs, so run-to-run variance is unknown.
- [I] Pass@1 on 15 solutions per approach (p. 7–8) is too small to support the performance ranking (e.g. 0.87 vs 0.53).
- [I] Internal inconsistencies:
  - Few-shot Pass@1 is 0.86 in the introduction (p. 1) and 0.87 in Table V (p. 8).
  - An odds ratio is not a percentage, but the paper expresses ORs as percentages (OR 0.0005 written as "0.05% of the odds", p. 6). Under that convention, the largest bug OR in Table II (0.019, p. 8) is 1.9%, not "≤ 0.19%" as stated in Finding 7 (p. 9).
  - Several severity percentages in the text do not match Fig. 5. Examples: zero-shot introductory critical is 5.0% in the text (p. 5) but 6.6 in Fig. 5 (p. 7); few-shot introductory values (critical 9.8%, major 40.2%, p. 5) do not appear in Fig. 5, where that bar is empty (p. 7); fine-tuned competition minor is 30% in the text (p. 6) but Fig. 5 shows 40.0 (p. 7).
  - The code-smell paragraph says "a bug in a few-shot approach is half as likely as a bug in a human solution" (p. 7), mixing bugs with smells.
  - The limitations say "GPT-4" (p. 10) while the model is GPT-4o (p. 4).
- [I] Top-p = 1.0 is described as "ensuring the most probable token distributions were used" (p. 4); top-p = 1.0 in fact applies no nucleus truncation. Minor, but it shows imprecise reporting of the generation setup.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Few-shot prompts contain baseline solutions (p. 4). Possible training-data contamination with APPS (not discussed). Train/test disjointness for fine-tuning not reported (p. 4). The human baseline includes many solutions per question, while LLMs produce one, so issue counts per question are not comparable unless normalised. The normalisation is not fully specified (p. 5).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): [A] Python, algorithmic problems, one model family (p. 10). [I] Single-function stdin/stdout programs say little about multi-file applications, UIs or vibe-coded apps.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [A] SonarQube rules and effort estimates are proxies (p. 10). [I] Static "bugs" and "code smells" from the default profile are only a partial measure of maintainability. Effort-to-fix is SonarQube's rule-based remediation estimate, not a measured effort.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [V] No CIs and no multiple-comparison correction (p. 8). [I] Odds ratios of 0.00 imply zero cells, where ORs are undefined without correction. A large Cliff's delta (−0.50) that is not significant suggests small or tied samples for the fine-tuned introductory set (p. 8).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Replication package with scripts on Zenodo, public dataset, model version and decoding parameters reported (p. 4, p. 11). [I] Sample sizes per condition, fine-tuning hyper-parameters, the exact SonarQube version and the OR test are missing. Fine-tuned GPT-4o weights are proprietary, so exact regeneration may be impossible.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]:
  - Explore parameter tuning (p. 10).
  - Use PEFT and data pruning instead of costly full fine-tuning (p. 9).
  - Study quality–performance–cost trade-offs in different domains (p. 10).
  - Try RAG and other LLMs; add more languages and quality metrics (p. 10).
  - Add a component that checks solution performance (p. 10).
  - Study links to educational outcomes (p. 10).
- Suggested by us [I]:
  - Report static quality only for solutions that pass the tests, so quality and correctness are evaluated jointly.
  - Use several samples per task with variance reporting.
  - Use a baseline of maintained, production-style human code.
  - Apply the same SonarQube pipeline to multi-file, application-level outputs (e.g. vibe-coded web apps) instead of single-function programs.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ3 (primary), RQ4, RQ2 (minor), RQ5.
- How it informs our work [I]:
  - It is a peer-reviewed (ESEM) direct comparison of LLM vs human code quality using SonarQube. It is a candidate template for the code-quality arm of a reconstruction study: default quality profile, bugs, smells, severity and remediation effort.
  - It shows that static quality and functional correctness can diverge sharply: the fine-tuned model has the best quality metrics but the lowest Pass@1. Any evaluation of reconstructed applications must therefore measure fidelity and quality jointly.
  - Its weaknesses are useful design lessons for RQ4/RQ5: baseline leakage, unreported N, tiny correctness sample, and no CIs or multiple-comparison correction.
  - Relevance is medium rather than high because the tasks are algorithmic snippets, not applications reconstructed from observable behaviour.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ3 | GPT-4o solutions (zero-shot, few-shot, fine-tuned) had far lower odds of SonarQube-flagged bugs than APPS human solutions at all difficulty levels (OR 0.00–0.019, all p<0.001; the 0.00 implies a zero cell, so the minimum is not a real estimate) | 8 | V | weak (single model and study; N per group not reported; few-shot prompt contains baseline solutions) |
| RQ3 | Code-smell (maintainability) differences were mixed: zero-shot had 3.57× the odds of a smell vs human on introductory tasks, while fine-tuned had fewer smells; several comparisons were not significant | 8 | V | weak |
| RQ3 | SonarQube-estimated fix effort was lower for LLM code on introductory/interview tasks but not on competition tasks (human 6.95 min vs few-shot 7.33, fine-tuned 7.60) | 7 | V | weak |
| RQ3 | On competition-level problems LLM outputs carried more critical-severity issues than human code | 6 | A | weak |
| RQ2 | Functional correctness diverged from static quality: Pass@1 human 1.0, few-shot 0.87, zero-shot 0.53, fine-tuned 0.47 (fine-tuned had the best quality metrics) | 8 | V | weak (15 solutions per approach) |
| RQ4 | Comparison used SonarQube default profile, odds ratios, and Mann-Whitney U with Cliff's delta, without CIs or multiple-comparison correction | 5, 8 | V | moderate |
| RQ4 | The few-shot prompt included the human reference solutions of the same question, so few-shot vs human is not an independent comparison | 4 | I | moderate (directly from method description) |
| RQ5 | Authors call for other LLMs, more languages and metrics, RAG and cost–quality trade-off studies | 10 | A | weak |

## 14. Key quotes
> "LLM-generated code has fewer bugs and requires less effort to fix them overall." (p. 1)

> "the fine-tuned model solutions lost performance (0.47) compared to the few-shot model (0.86) in Pass@1" (p. 1)

> "current AI models may better avoid functional bugs than address structural code quality concerns." (p. 9)

> "Since the questions are not intended for use in a professional environment, the solutions may be prepared to be correct in the first place, leaving quality metrics as a low priority or even unobserved." (p. 9)

- Reading coverage: all 12 PDF pages read, including references. Figures 4–6 and Tables I–V were checked on the PDF images (pp. 6–8) because text extraction scrambled them. Figure 1 (architecture) was not inspected in detail; it is descriptive only.

  - The exact number of solutions per dataset is not reported. This is the main obstacle to judging statistical strength.

# Understanding the Code and Architectural Smells Generated by LLMs and Autonomous Agents

- Authors: Zhu, Yuecai; Tsantalis, Nikolaos; Rigby, Peter C.
- Year / venue: 2026, Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (published)
- DOI: 10.1145/3832783.3834413 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3832783.3834413
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index). Our PDF is arXiv 2605.02741v1 (4 May 2026), titled "AI-Generated Smells: An Analysis of Code and Architecture in LLM- and Agent-Driven Development" (p. 1). The title differs from metadata.json, but authors and abstract match, so we treat it as the preprint of the ASE paper. The published version may differ. DOI–PDF link: **probable**, not confirmed. `rlab`'s identity "match" rests on the arXiv id that `metadata.json` itself associates with the ACM DOI. `oa_pdf_url` points to the ACM DL, but our text was taken from arXiv. The ACM version was not fetched or compared.

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
Audit the code smells (technical debt) in code produced by single LLMs and by a multi-agent system, and analyse how moving from single-file algorithmic tasks to multi-file applications changes the density and kinds of smells [A] (p. 1).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- RQ1: To what extent do code-generating agents introduce code smells in standard coding tasks? RQ2: What taxonomy of code smells do code-generating agents most often show? RQ3: How does the complexity of the target architecture affect smell prevalence, and can prompt strategies mitigate it? [V] (p. 1). These are the paper's own RQs, not our project RQs.
- No formal hypotheses. Note: the results section maps RQ2 and RQ3 differently from the introduction (RQ2 = complex-system smells, RQ3 = drivers of decay) (p. 6, p. 8, p. 9).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: exploratory, two-experiment static-analysis study [V] (p. 3). Experiment I: five LLMs generate Python solutions for algorithmic problems under zero-shot and few-shot prompts; smells compared with human solutions [V] (p. 3, p. 4). Experiment II: MetaGPT multi-agent framework (Qwen-Coder 480B backend) generates full Python applications for 5 scenarios, each at 4 increasingly detailed requirement stages; smells related to size, scenario and stage [V] (p. 5, p. 8).
- Approach / model / intervention: Exp I models: Gemini 2.5 Pro, Llama 3.3 70B, deepseek-coder-v2 16B, qwen3-coder 30B and 480B [V] (p. 3). Zero-shot prompt replicates Santa et al.; few-shot prompt adds role, output rules and a boilerplate `solution` method [V] (p. 4). Exp II prompts require OOP and modular files because preliminary trials produced monolithic "God Class" scripts [V] (p. 5). Scenarios: Crossy Road game, Flashcard app, Pacman, Personal Finance (CLI + web dashboard), Online Bookstore backend [V] (p. 5).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: Exp I — one randomly sampled verified human Python submission per problem; zero-shot as prompt baseline [V] (p. 4). Exp II — no human or alternative-agent baseline; comparison only across scenarios and stages [V] (p. 5, p. 9).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): CodeContests dataset (AlphaCode) for Exp I; author-written product requirements for Exp II [V] (p. 1, p. 3, p. 5).
- Sample size (N) and unit: Exp I — 90 problems, 5 LLMs × 2 prompt conditions, plus 90 human solutions; unit = one generated .py file per problem [V] (p. 4). Exp II — 5 scenarios × 4 stages [V] (p. 5); the resulting number of repositories (20 implied) and the number of generation runs per prompt are not reported explicitly. [I] n ≈ 20 is supported by the reported Spearman p-values. Under the usual t-approximation, ρ = 0.53 → p = 0.017 and ρ = 0.59 → p = 0.007 (Table 3, p. 9) correspond to n ≈ 19–20 (our calculation). [I] Each stage is probably an independent generation, not an evolution of the previous codebase, because the four stage prompts are self-contained (p. 5).
- Sampling / selection method: 90 problems "randomly sampled" (p. 4), later described as a "stratified sample" balanced across Easy/Medium/Hard (p. 9) [V]. Model selection to span dense vs MoE, proprietary vs open, and parameter scale [V] (p. 3).
- Data availability (public? link?): replication package at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19245562 with sampling scripts, Exp I scripts, Exp II prompts and analysis scripts [V] (p. 10). Generated repositories announced as a benchmark dataset "released alongside this paper" [A] (p. 5).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: each solution saved as a .py file and analysed with PyExamine; counts per smell type aggregated [V] (p. 4). Exp II repositories also measured with cloc (TLoC), total number of files (ToF) and Agent Action Count (AAC) [V] (p. 5). No iterative "validate and correct" loop in Exp I (budget) [V] (p. 9). Temperature, sampling settings, model quantisation/hosting, PyExamine version and thresholds: not reported. Results for AAC: not reported. The factor "ALpF" in Table 3 is not defined in the text (p. 9).
- Code availability: scripts in the Zenodo package (p. 10).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
  - PyExamine smell counts at three levels: code-level (e.g. Long Method, Long File, High Cyclomatic Complexity), structural (class/object level, e.g. Too Many Branches, High Response for a Class, Temporal Field) and architectural (e.g. Unstable Dependency, Scattered Functionality, Potential Improper API Usage) [V] (p. 3, p. 7, p. 8). Chosen as a comprehensive, "un-opinionated", static and repeatable Python smell detector, and to separate structural smells from superficial linting issues counted by SonarQube [A] (p. 2, p. 4).
  - TLoC and ToF as project size/complexity [V] (p. 5).
  - Feature Envy and Potential Shotgun Surgery were excluded from Exp I interpretation after a manual audit found systematic false positives; Long Method and Long File were judged high precision [V] (p. 6). The size of this audit and precision values are not reported.
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): Exp I — raw counts only, no statistical test, no normalisation by code size [V] (p. 7). Exp II — Spearman's ρ (continuous factors) and Kruskal-Wallis H (Scenario, Stage), p < 0.05; no multiple-comparison correction, no confidence intervals [V] (p. 8, p. 9). Functional correctness of generated code: not measured or reported.

## 7. Key findings
1. Exp I: Long Method counts were higher for larger LLMs than for humans — zero-shot Qwen Coder 480B 11, Qwen Coder 30B 7, Gemini 2.5 Pro 5, deepseek 2, Llama 3 70B 0, human 1 (across 90 problems) — [V] (p. 7, Table 1).
2. Exp I: Temporal Field appeared only in human solutions (4 instances), never in LLM output — [V] (p. 6, p. 7).
3. Exp I: few-shot prompting did not reduce Long Method (Qwen 480B 11 → 13; Gemini 5 → 8) — [V] (p. 6, p. 7, Table 2).
4. Exp I interpretation: a "Reasoning-Complexity Trade-off" — more capable models produce more procedural bloat; larger models' failed solutions had more Long Methods — [A] (p. 6, p. 7). The failed/passing split is not shown in any table.
5. Exp II: ranked by mean count over all Exp II repositories (pooled), the most prevalent smells were Too Many Branches, High Response for a Class, Potential Improper API Usage, Scattered Functionality and Unstable Dependency — [V] (p. 8, Figure 1 caption; p. 7). The authors add that these smells appear consistently "across all stages and scenarios" — [A] (p. 7); Figure 1 pools repositories and no per-stage or per-scenario breakdown is shown.
6. Exp II: TLoC correlated with code-level (ρ = 0.53, p = 0.017), structural (ρ = 0.59, p = 0.007) and architectural smell counts (ρ = 0.94, p < 0.001); ToF with architectural smells ρ = 0.72 (p < 0.001) — [V] (p. 8, p. 9, Table 3).
7. Exp II: scenario affected architectural smells (H = 9.86, p = 0.043); requirement stage had no significant effect on any smell level (p > 0.8) — [V] (p. 8, p. 9, Table 3).
8. Authors' framing: a "Volume-Quality Inverse Law" and a "Modular Mirage" (files are separated but behaviour is fragmented); agents act like "junior developers" lacking architectural foresight — [A] (p. 8, p. 9).
9. Abstract/introduction claim that functional correctness is decoupled from quality ("running code is just as likely to be structurally flawed as failed code") — [A] (p. 1, p. 2). No supporting data is reported in the results.

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] No iterative debug/repair loop in Exp I; first-pass code only (p. 9, p. 10).
- [A] Exp I uses 90 problems, not the full dataset; may miss long-tail problem types; authors plan to scale up "to verify the statistical significance of these findings" (p. 9).
- [A] Exp II uses only MetaGPT; findings may be specific to its SOP-based paradigm; other tools (SpecKit, Cursor Composer) may differ (p. 9, p. 10).
- [A] Small sample, so non-parametric tests were used (p. 8).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] Central claims rest on very small counts. Exp I differences are a handful of smell instances over 90 files (e.g. 11 vs 1 Long Method), with no test, no per-LoC normalisation and no variance across runs (p. 7). Treat as descriptive.
- [I] The "Volume-Quality Inverse Law" correlates smell *counts* with code size (p. 8, p. 9). More code mechanically yields more smell instances, so ρ = 0.94 does not show that larger code is worse per line. The paper says size metrics allow density normalisation (p. 5) but reports no density analysis.
- [I] The claims that functional correctness does not mitigate decay (p. 1, p. 2) are not backed by any reported correctness measure; Exp II apps were not executed or tested at all as far as the paper reports.
- [I] The "longitudinal"/"architectural rot" framing (p. 2, p. 5) is questionable: the four stage prompts are self-contained (p. 5), and the paper does not say that each stage evolves the previous codebase. It may be four independent generations.
- [I] Exp II has n ≈ 20, one LLM backend, one framework, no human or single-agent baseline, and 15 significance tests without correction (p. 9); the "near-perfect predictor" wording overstates a single small sample.
- [I] Internal inconsistencies: RQ numbering differs between introduction and results; "random" vs "stratified" sampling; "ALpF" undefined; smell abbreviations in Exp I (EC, HFI) are not expanded (p. 1, p. 4, p. 6, p. 7, p. 9).
- [I] PyExamine validity: two smell types were dropped as false positives after an unquantified audit (p. 6); no precision figures for the architectural smells that drive the main conclusion.
- [I] Model inference settings (temperature, quantisation; model names suggest local deployment) are not reported, which limits reproducibility.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): size confounds smell counts (Exp II); CodeContests problems may be in model training data (not discussed); prompts for Exp II were engineered to force modularity after preliminary trials (p. 5).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): Python only; competitive programming tasks (Exp I); five small app scenarios with a single agent framework and one LLM (Exp II) (p. 5, p. 9, p. 10).
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): maintainability is equated with PyExamine smell counts; no human assessment of maintainability; FE and PSS judged unreliable (p. 6).
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): no tests in Exp I; small n and no correction in Exp II; no repeated generations, so model randomness is not estimated (p. 7, p. 8, p. 9).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): Zenodo package with scripts and prompts (p. 10); generation hyper-parameters not reported. Authors note Gemini 3.1 was used for editorial purposes (p. 10).

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: architecturally-aware agents (explicit "Architect" role, constitutional design principles); refactoring agents that detect and fix AI-specific smells such as the "Modular Mirage"; longitudinal benchmarks of continuous software evolution; metrics for semantic cohesion (p. 10); extend the benchmark to other agent platforms (p. 9); scale Exp I to the full dataset (p. 9).
- Suggested by us [I]: repeat Exp II with smell density per KLoC, multiple runs per prompt, a human-written reference implementation of the same apps, and functional tests, so that "correctness vs quality" is actually measured.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ3 (main), RQ1, RQ4.
- How it informs our work [I]: Exp II is close to our setting: complete small applications (games, GUI tools, web backend) generated by an agent from natural-language requirements. It gives a smell taxonomy for agent-built apps (God-class branching, unstable dependencies, scattered functionality) that a reconstruction study could measure. Its evidence is weak (preprint version, tiny n, count-based statistics, no correctness data), so it should support hypotheses rather than conclusions, and it illustrates RQ4 weaknesses (no size normalisation, no baselines).

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ3 | In 90 algorithmic tasks, larger LLMs produced more Long Method smells than humans (Qwen-480B 11, Gemini 5, human 1, zero-shot); humans alone produced Temporal Field (4) | 7 | V | weak |
| RQ3 | Few-shot prompting with coding standards did not reduce Long Method smells (Qwen-480B 11→13, Gemini 5→8) | 6, 7 | V | weak |
| RQ3 | MetaGPT-generated apps mainly show Too Many Branches, High Response for a Class, Potential Improper API Usage, Scattered Functionality and Unstable Dependency smells | 7, 8 | V | weak |
| RQ3 | In MetaGPT apps, architectural smell counts correlate with total LoC (ρ=0.94, p<0.001); more detailed requirement stages had no significant effect (p>0.8) | 8, 9 | V | weak |
| RQ1 | Multi-agent framework (MetaGPT + Qwen-Coder 480B) generated full multi-file Python apps (games, flashcards, finance dashboard, bookstore backend) from staged NL requirements; needed explicit modularity prompts to avoid monolithic scripts | 5 | V | weak |
| RQ4 | Smell counts are not normalised by size, Exp I has no statistical tests, and functional correctness is not measured despite claims about it | 1, 7, 8 | I | weak |
| RQ5 | Authors call for semantic-cohesion metrics, longitudinal evolution benchmarks and architecture-aware/refactoring agents | 10 | A | weak |

## 14. Key quotes
> "functional correctness is decoupled from quality—running code is just as likely to be structurally flawed as failed code" (p. 2)

> "TLoC exhibited a near-perfect positive correlation with architectural smells" (p. 8)

> "the specificity of requirements (Stage) had no statistical impact on any smell category" (p. 8)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: all 11 PDF pages read, including tables, threats to validity, conclusion, data availability and references. Figure 1 (box plot, p. 8) read from its caption only; no numeric values extracted from it.
- Uncertainties: whether the ASE published version differs from this arXiv v1 (different title); exact number of Exp II repositories and runs; meaning of "ALpF"; whether Exp II stages evolve the same codebase. Evidence strength set to weak throughout because of small samples, count-only statistics and missing correctness data, even though the venue (ASE) is peer-reviewed.

# Comparing the Quality of Code Generated by Vibe Coding Tools

- Authors: Mota, Gustavo da; Gama, Kiev
- Year / venue: 2026, arXiv (preprint)
- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2608.16302 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16302
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

Note on the source: arXiv v1 (arXiv:2608.16302, 17 Aug 2026), 7 pages. **Not peer-reviewed as far as we can tell**: the page header names the 40th Brazilian Symposium on Software Engineering (SBES 2026), Innovative Ideas and Emerging Results track (p. 2), but the artifact link is "anonymized for review" (p. 6), so this appears to be a submitted version; acceptance is not stated. Treated as a preprint (`venue_kind: preprint`).

## 1. Research objective
- [A] To obtain "initial evidence about the structural quality of code generated by vibe coding tools from the same requirements specification", explicitly "rather than declaring one tool superior" (p. 2).
- [A] Motivation: evaluating "entire AI-generated applications" rather than isolated functions or algorithmic solutions (p. 1).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [V] RQ1: "How do vibe coding tools differ in the number and severity of code smells detected in web applications generated from the same set of requirements?" (p. 2)
- No hypotheses (exploratory) (p. 2).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Exploratory comparative design; unit of analysis is one project generated by a platform from an identical prompt (p. 2).
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] One zero-shot prompt (no example code) derived from the "Nature Park Wildlife App" exercise (wildlife sighting registration, safety reports, notification subscriptions, geolocated map) (p. 2). Each tool received the same prompt "with no additional instructions or manual corrections"; repeated three times per tool (p. 2). Each project analysed independently with SonarQube (p. 2).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] The three tools are compared with each other (Lovable, v0, Replit) (p. 2). No human-written reference implementation; no non-AI baseline.

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] Nine generated web applications: Lovable (tanstack_start_ts template, gpt-engineer-app agent), v0 (Next.js 16.2.4), Replit (Replit Agent, Node.js 24); generated 6-21 May 2026 on free tiers (p. 2).
- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 9 projects, 3 per tool (p. 2). NCLOC totals: Lovable 17,081; v0 27,583; Replit 48,411 (p. 5). Issues: 390, 254, 463 (total 1,107) (p. 5).
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Tools chosen as widely used, fully web-based app generators with free tiers sufficient for the experiments (p. 2). Three runs per tool limited by free-tier token credits and time (p. 6). No power or sample-size rationale beyond this.
- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Full prompt, source code of all nine projects and full SonarQube reports at an anonymised 4open.science link (p. 6). We did not open it.

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] SonarQube (version and quality profile/rule set: not reported) on each project (p. 2). Tool versions not public; generation window and build identifiers reported instead (p. 2). Tags (39 distinct) grouped by the authors into five clusters: Semantic, Technical Quality, Security, Technological Context, Language/Ecosystem (Table 1, p. 3). How the grouping was decided: not reported. Whether template, scaffolding or vendored UI-component code was excluded from analysis: not reported.
- Code availability: [V] Generated code and SonarQube reports in the artefact package (p. 6). No analysis scripts mentioned.

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] SonarQube issues by type (code smell, bug, vulnerability; hotspots in Table 6), severity (MINOR/MAJOR/CRITICAL), rules and tags, remediation effort in minutes (as a technical-debt estimate), duplicated-line density, cyclomatic and cognitive complexity, NCLOC (p. 2, p. 3, p. 5). Raw and per-KLOC values reported because code volume differs while required functionality is the same (p. 2). SonarQube chosen as widely adopted in industry and research (p. 2).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): not reported (descriptive only). Standard deviation reported only for code smells per project (Lovable 62.1, v0 7.0, Replit 20.3) (p. 6). Cyclomatic complexity is listed as collected (p. 1, p. 2) but its values are not reported.

## 7. Key findings
1. [V] Per KLOC, Lovable had 22.83 issues vs 9.21 (v0) and 9.56 (Replit); remediation effort 220.77 min/KLOC vs 34.12 and 34.87 (Table 6, p. 5).
2. [V] Raw totals: Lovable 390 issues / 3,771 min effort; v0 254 / 941; Replit 463 / 1,688 (Table 6, p. 5). Lovable effort is about 4.0x v0's (p. 6).
3. [V] Lovable's issues are almost all code smells (389 of 390) and mostly MINOR (85.6%) (p. 3, p. 5); rule S1874 (deprecated APIs) accounts for 204 occurrences (p. 3, p. 5).
   [A] S1874 accounts for more than half of Lovable's remediation effort (p. 6); this share cannot be derived from the reported tables.
4. [V] Replit produced the most code (48,411 NCLOC), about 60% duplicated lines vs <=7% (v0) and 0% (Lovable), and the highest MAJOR share (213 issues, 46%); Replit had no CRITICAL issues, Lovable and v0 1.0% and 1.2% (p. 4, p. 5, p. 6).
5. [V] Bugs per tool are few: 1 (Lovable), 5 (v0), 8 (Replit); security hotspots 6, 10, 30 (Table 6, p. 5).
6. [V] Within-tool variation is large: Lovable's wildlife-whisperer-app had 59 issues and 215 min effort vs 167/1,782 and 164/1,774 for the other two Lovable projects (Table 3, p. 3).
7. [A] v0 "emerged as the most balanced alternative" (p. 6); Lovable "may produce code that looks clean but relies on APIs whose reliability ... has already been questioned" (p. 6); Replit's productivity gain "may come with a more significant structural debt over the medium term" (p. 6).
8. [A] The deprecated-API pattern is explained by LLMs over-representing API patterns prevalent at training time (p. 5, p. 6). This is a plausible literature-based explanation, not tested here.

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Static analysis (SonarQube) cannot definitively quantify code quality; only a subset of its checkers may reveal real flaws, which may inflate technical-debt indices (p. 6).
- [A] Only three projects per tool because of free-tier token limits and time; results are susceptible to anomalous outputs, as shown by Lovable's SD of 62.1 driven by one project (p. 6).
- [A] Platform opacity: no transparency on resource allocation in free tiers; lower-capacity models might be used at peak times ("speculation, not a claim") (p. 6).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] Sample size: n = 3 per tool and n = 9 overall, one prompt, one application domain (p. 2). With this N, tool differences cannot be separated from run-to-run variance; a single outlier project (Lovable's wildlife-whisperer-app, p. 3) changes the raw issue-count ranking (replacing its 59 issues with a sibling-like ~165 would lift Lovable to ~496, above Replit's 463), but not the remediation-effort ranking, since each other Lovable project alone (1,782 and 1,774 min) exceeds v0's three-project total of 941 min (p. 3, p. 5). All tool-level conclusions are hypotheses, not findings.
- [I] Functional fidelity is not checked: the paper never verifies that the nine apps run or implement the prompted requirements, while per-KLOC comparisons assume "the expected functionality of the projects is the same" (p. 2). Code volume and smell counts are hard to compare if the apps deliver different features.
- [I] Template and boilerplate confound: Lovable starts from a dated template (p. 2) and Replit's ~60% duplication (p. 4) may come from scaffolding or copied UI components. The paper does not say whether such code was excluded, so part of the measured "generated" quality may belong to templates. S1874 (deprecated APIs) is a likely candidate for template- or library-driven issues.
- [I] Lovable's effort lead (3,771 min total) is robust across 2 of 3 projects (1,782 and 1,774 min, p. 3) but is driven mainly by one rule, S1874, which per the authors accounts for more than half of the effort (p. 6); whether that rule reflects template code is unknown.
- [I] The text calls Replit's severity profile the "highest absolute and relative share of severe issues" (p. 4), yet Replit is the only tool with no CRITICAL issues (p. 5); "severe" here means MAJOR.
- [I] Tag-to-cluster mapping is author-defined without a stated procedure (p. 3); the "Security" cluster is only the `cwe` tag.
- [I] SonarQube version and rule profile not reported; free tiers only; no repeated analysis with a second tool.
- [I] The acknowledgements state that Claude generated "all the figures and tables" from the authors' specifications (p. 6). We re-computed the Table 6 per-KLOC values from the raw totals and they are consistent, but transcription errors elsewhere cannot be ruled out without the artefacts.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Templates/boilerplate not separated; platform model tier not controlled ([A] p. 6); different stacks per tool (TanStack Start, Next.js, Node) mean SonarQube rules apply differently.
- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] One prompt, one small CRUD-plus-map web app, free tiers, May 2026 platform versions; premium tiers may differ ([A] p. 6).
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [A] SonarQube issues are an auxiliary indicator, not a definitive quality measure (p. 6). [I] Remediation minutes are SonarQube defaults per rule, not observed effort; no maintainability task (e.g. change requests) measured.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No inferential statistics; n = 3 per group; high within-tool variance (p. 6).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Prompt, generated code and SonarQube reports shared (p. 6); generation window and build identifiers reported (p. 2). [I] SaaS platforms change continuously and are non-deterministic, so regeneration will not reproduce the same code; the shared code allows re-analysis only.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: substantially more iterations per tool; premium versions of the platforms; additional static analysis tools besides SonarQube (p. 6). Broader replications across varied contexts before definitive conclusions (p. 6).
- Suggested by us [I]: add functional verification (requirement-based acceptance tests) alongside static analysis; separate template/vendored code from generated code; use several prompts and app types; add maintainability tasks (implementing change requests) rather than only static indicators. For our project: this is the closest design to a vibe-coded application study and could be extended with a reference application (to measure fidelity) and a human-written baseline.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (whole-app generation with commercial vibe-coding platforms: Lovable, v0, Replit), RQ3 (SonarQube smells, duplication, remediation effort of vibe-coded apps), RQ4 (very small N, no functional check, single static tool), RQ5 (joint fidelity + quality evaluation missing).
- How it informs our work [I]: it evaluates complete web applications produced end-to-end by vibe-coding platforms from one NL specification, which is the closest setting in our set to rebuilding an app by vibe coding. It shows that quality profiles differ by platform and by run, but it does not measure functional fidelity, so it illustrates exactly the gap our RQ5 targets. Evidence weight is low (preprint, n = 9), relevance high.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | Commercial vibe-coding platforms (Lovable, v0, Replit) generated complete web apps from a single zero-shot NL prompt without manual correction | p. 2 | V | weak |
| RQ3 | Per KLOC, Lovable apps had 22.83 SonarQube issues vs 9.21 (v0) and 9.56 (Replit), and 220.77 vs about 34 min/KLOC remediation effort; mostly MINOR code smells driven by deprecated-API rule S1874 (204 occurrences) | p. 3, p. 5 | V | weak |
| RQ3 | Replit apps were the largest (48,411 NCLOC for 3 apps) with about 60% duplicated lines and 46% MAJOR-severity issues | p. 4, p. 5, p. 6 | V | weak |
| RQ3 | Authors suggest vibe-coding tools may systematically use outdated APIs because LLMs over-represent historical API patterns | p. 5, p. 6 | A | weak |
| RQ4 | Only 3 projects per tool (free-tier limits); one Lovable project differed strongly (59 vs 164-167 issues), code-smell SD 62.1 vs 7.0 and 20.3 | p. 3, p. 6 | V | weak |
| RQ4 | Quality measured only by SonarQube static analysis, which the authors note is an auxiliary indicator; no functional testing of the generated apps | p. 2, p. 6 | V | moderate |
| RQ5 | Authors call for more runs per tool, premium tiers and additional static analysers before definitive conclusions | p. 6 | A | weak |

## 14. Key quotes
> "Rather than declaring one tool superior to the others, the goal of this study is to obtain initial evidence about the structural quality of code generated by vibe coding tools" (p. 2)

> "only three projects were generated per tool — a volume still susceptible to anomalous outputs" (p. 6)

> "reported productivity gains do not necessarily reflect structural quality" (p. 5)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: whole paper read (pp. 1-7 incl. references). Figures 1-9 checked in the text; page 5 (Table 6, Figures 6-9) also viewed in the PDF to confirm values. Artefact package not opened.
- Uncertainties: publication status (SBES 2026 header but anonymised "for review" artefact link); SonarQube version/profile; whether generated apps work. Lovable's "58 code smells" for wildlife-whisperer-app (p. 6) vs 59 issues in Table 3 (p. 3) is consistent if that project contains the single bug, but this is not stated.
