### C1. Does AI assistance harm maintainability? he2026speed vs borg2026echoes
- **Side A** [V]: Cursor adoption in 806 OSS repositories raised total SonarQube static-analysis warnings by +30.26% and total cognitive complexity by +41.64% relative to matched controls (Borusyak DiD) [@he2026speed, p. 7]. The complexity effect stays significant after controlling for codebase size in the GMM (0.086, p<0.01) [@he2026speed, p. 8].
- **Side B** [V]: When a second developer evolved AI-co-developed code without AI, there was no significant difference in completion time [@borg2026echoes, p. 33], CodeHealth (8.49 vs 8.44) [@borg2026echoes, p. 38] or test coverage [@borg2026echoes, p. 35]. The only "significant" maintainability effect, a Bayesian +0.10 CodeHealth for code from habitual AI users, favours AI [@borg2026echoes, p. 39].
- **Differences**:
  - Data and population: real-world OSS repositories with ≥10 stars [@he2026speed, p. 4] vs one 2 KLoC Java/Spring Boot task done by 151 volunteer professionals [@borg2026echoes, p. 19; @borg2026echoes, p. 64].
  - Tool generation: an agentic IDE (Cursor Composer/agent) [@he2026speed, p. 2] vs late-2024 assistants (Copilot, ChatGPT, Cursor) [@borg2026echoes, p. 3; @borg2026echoes, p. 60].
  - Metric: repository-total warnings and cognitive complexity, which scale with code size [@he2026speed, p. 5] vs a LoC-weighted file-level CodeHealth average plus a second developer's evolution time [@borg2026echoes, p. 13].
  - Time: monthly panel of up to about 20 months [@he2026speed, p. 5] vs a single hand-off task.
  - Robustness: he2026speed's quality effects turn negative and non-significant under the Callaway–Sant'Anna estimator (warnings −10.49%, complexity −3.80%) [@he2026speed, p. 16]. borg2026echoes is underpowered (75 of 128 planned participants; 80% power only for d≈0.66) [@borg2026echoes, p. 19].
- **Partial agreement** [V]: borg2026echoes' observational Phase 1 also found more duplication (23% vs 11%), more complex conditionals and very large code-volume outliers in AI-assisted code [@borg2026echoes, p. 30; @borg2026echoes, p. 46]. With size controlled, he2026speed finds no direct Cursor effect on warnings [@he2026speed, p. 8].
- **Possible explanation** [I]: the two results need not conflict. Both fit "AI adds more code, and project-level totals rise with it, while per-file health and the short-term effort of the next developer are not clearly worse". The he2026speed effect depends on the estimator, and borg2026echoes can rule out only large effects. Neither study settles the question.

### C2. Fewer or more static-analysis issues in LLM code? molison2025llm vs he2026speed
- **Side A** [V]: GPT-4o solutions had far lower odds of SonarQube-flagged "bugs" than APPS human solutions (OR 0.00–0.019) [@molison2025llm, p. 8], and lower SonarQube fix effort on introductory and interview tasks [@molison2025llm, p. 7].
- **Side B** [V]: Cursor adoption raised repository SonarQube warnings by +30.26% [@he2026speed, p. 7].
- **Differences**:
  - Unit: per-solution odds of an issue in single-file stdin/stdout programs [@molison2025llm, p. 5] vs monthly repository totals [@he2026speed, p. 5].
  - Baseline: competitive-programming submissions written for correctness, not maintainability [@molison2025llm, p. 9] vs matched non-adopting repositories, which may themselves use other AI tools [@he2026speed, p. 7].
  - Metric: the SonarQube "bug" category vs all reliability, maintainability and security warnings.
  - Leakage: molison2025llm's few-shot prompt contains the human reference solutions [@molison2025llm, p. 4].
  - Time: GPT-4o in 2024 vs Cursor agents in 2024–2025.
- **Possible explanation** [I]: the results are not comparable. Both use SonarQube, but the units, baselines and code types differ, so neither one refutes the other. molison2025llm's smell results are themselves mixed: zero-shot code had 3.57x the odds of a smell on introductory tasks [@molison2025llm, p. 8].

### C3. Which instrument measures the quality of AI code? zhu2026understanding vs SonarQube-based studies
- **Side A** [A]: zhu2026understanding chose PyExamine to separate structural and architectural smells from the "superficial linting issues" counted by SonarQube [@zhu2026understanding, p. 2; @zhu2026understanding, p. 4]. It found more Long Method smells in larger LLMs' code than in human code [@zhu2026understanding, p. 7].
- **Side B** [V]: SonarQube-based studies report fewer issues in LLM code [@molison2025llm, p. 8], a platform-dependent issue density (22.83 vs about 9 issues/KLOC) [@mota2026comparing, p. 5], or more warnings with adoption [@he2026speed, p. 7].
- **Context** [A]: technical-debt tools disagree on what counts as real debt [@ehsani2026faster, p. 5], and SonarQube and general linters were not designed for LLM-specific debt [@ehsani2026faster, p. 22]. mota2026comparing calls SonarQube an auxiliary indicator only [@mota2026comparing, p. 6]. borg2026echoes argues that CodeHealth outperforms the SonarQube Maintainability Rating; note that its first author works for CodeScene, the vendor of CodeHealth [@borg2026echoes, p. 4; @borg2026echoes, p. 75].
- **Differences**: the tools differ (PyExamine, SonarQube, CodeHealth, MI), and so do the task types (algorithmic snippets, generated web apps, OSS repositories). zhu2026understanding's Exp I counts are small, unnormalised and untested [@zhu2026understanding, p. 7].
- **Possible explanation** [I]: the direction of "LLM vs human code quality" may depend on the measuring instrument. The field has no validated, size-normalised maintainability measure for AI-generated code.

### C4. Does iterative feedback or self-repair help? pan2026functional vs tran2026vibe / zhou2025declarui / wu2026looks
- **Side A** [V]: On GPT-5.2, three one-shot strategies all lowered the aggregate non-functional score without raising functional correctness: self-repair, environment repair and planning (NF 46.1–49.9% vs 57.1% at baseline) [@pan2026functional, p. 8].
- **Side B**:
  - [V] Browser self-testing during generation correlates with accuracy across 16 models (r = 0.72) [@tran2026vibe, p. 7].
  - [V] Removing DeclarUI's page-transition graph plus refinement loop cuts navigation coverage to 23.1% [@zhou2025declarui, p. 10]. Its compile success is 98% vs 74–76% for raw MLLMs [@zhou2025declarui, p. 9].
  - [V]/[A] A tsc + vite verify-repair loop gives 100% build success for all six models [@wu2026looks, p. 6]. The authors attribute this to the loop [@wu2026looks, p. 12].
### C6. Multi-agent / agentic frameworks: MetaGPT fails in liu2026benchmarking but leads in mock2026vibe
- **Side A** [V]: MetaGPT nearly always fails on E2EDev (0–5.4% Req.Acc) [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 6]. Multi-agent frameworks "do not consistently improve" over a plain LLM (by our count, 9 of 24 cells higher [I]) [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 6].
- **Side B** [V]: Agentic MetaGPT X runs had the highest test pass rate (mean 94.58%) [@mock2026vibe, p. 25; @mock2026vibe, p. 41]. zhu2026understanding generated complete multi-file apps with MetaGPT, but only after adding explicit modularity prompts [@zhu2026understanding, p. 5].
- **Differences**:
  - Task size: a two-function string task [@mock2026vibe, p. 12] vs 46 multi-requirement web apps.
  - Backbone: GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4 [@mock2026vibe, p. 17] vs older or smaller backbones such as GPT-4o and Qwen2.5 [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 5].
  - Product: MetaGPT X web interface vs the open-source framework.
  - Evaluation: 12 runs pooled vs 46 projects x 3 runs.
- **Possible explanation** [I]: framework value depends on the backbone and the task scale. mock2026vibe's agentic advantage is confounded with the newer model generation.

### C7. Security of generated code: pan2026functional vs zhao2025vibe
- **Side A** [V]: Reference-normalised security averages 87.40% and is the strongest non-functional dimension [@pan2026functional, p. 6].
- **Side B** [V]: 79.3% of the functionally correct solutions of the best agent fail targeted security tests, and SecPass is only 3.8–12.9% [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6].
- **Differences**: pan2026functional counts high-risk static findings relative to the reference, and the score can reward incomplete code. zhao2025vibe runs 3.5 targeted security tests per task for a known historical CWE [@zhao2025vibe, p. 5]. The tasks also differ: whole-repository generation vs security-sensitive feature patches.
- **Possible explanation** [I]: the two instruments measure different things, a static absence of flagged patterns vs exploit-relevant behaviour. "Secure" cannot be compared across them.

### C8. More code or less code? Rebuilds are smaller, but assisted development adds code
- **Side A** [V]: Reconstructions are much smaller than their references. In bai2026recreationworld they are 89.4% smaller with 92.3% fewer files (4 of 10 models; desktop and Android only) [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15]. In yang2026programbench they are shorter (median 1,173 vs 3,068 lines) and use fewer files [@yang2026programbench, p. 9].
- **Side B** [V]:
  - Cursor adoption raises lines added by +281.3% in month 1 [@he2026speed, p. 8].
  - AI-assisted Task 1 code produced outliers of up to 10,788 lines [@borg2026echoes, p. 30].
  - In MetaGPT apps, architectural smell counts track code size (ρ = 0.94) [@zhu2026understanding, p. 8].
  - The visual-fidelity leader writes 1,441 LoC vs 668 for GPT-5 [@wu2026looks, p. 7].
- **Differences**: rebuilds from scratch scored against a behavioural oracle of a mature original, vs incremental additions to existing projects or apps generated from a spec.
- **Possible explanation** [I]: reconstructions under-implement the original, which is consistent with low full-pass rates. Assisted development adds volume. Size therefore carries opposite signals in the two settings, and size-driven quality metrics (smell counts, totals) must be normalised before comparison.

### C9. Apparent disagreements that come from different constructs (do not pool)
- **"Vibe coding" means different things** [V]:
  - fawzy2026vibe: natural-language prompting plus re-prompting with minimal review [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 1].
  - asdaque2026novice: a supervised agent workflow, operationalised as opening agentic PRs [@asdaque2026novice, p. 1]. Its authors warn that the findings may not hold under a broader definition [@asdaque2026novice, p. 4].
  - mock2026vibe: human-written TDD tests plus scripted prompts that participants could not modify [@mock2026vibe, p. 15].
  - he2026speed: Cursor configuration files committed to a repository (intent-to-treat) [@he2026speed, p. 4].
  - ehsani2026faster: a driver of fast-integration debt in mostly grey sources [@ehsani2026faster, p. 17].
  - [I] These are different interventions. Their results should not be pooled as "effects of vibe coding".
- **Fidelity scores are not comparable** [V]:
  - 58.06% average of programmatic and VLM channels [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
  - 36.35 Final Score (0.7 IFS + 0.3 VFS) [@chen2025iwr, p. 8].
  - 49.15% cumulative workflows [@kim2026programdistill, p. 11].
  - 53.75% Req.Acc with `data-testid` anchors [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 6].
  - 27.8% UI-agent accuracy with half credit for PARTIAL [@lu2025webgen, p. 8].
  - 61.77% workflows passing at ≥90% of substeps [@tran2026vibe, p. 6].
  - 0% resolved / 3% almost [@yang2026programbench, p. 6].
  - [I] Each figure uses a different oracle, input, application type and model generation. Do not rank across them.

### C10. Same model family builds or judges the benchmark and is evaluated (possible bias; untested)
- **Overlap and the same family wins** [V]:
  - yang2026programbench: Claude Sonnet 4.5 wrote the tests [@yang2026programbench, p. 3], and Claude models top the leaderboard [@yang2026programbench, p. 31].
  - tran2026vibe: GPT-5 drafted the specs [@tran2026vibe, p. 3], and GPT-5.3-Codex ranks first [@tran2026vibe, p. 6]. The canonical judge is Claude Sonnet 4.5 [@tran2026vibe, p. 4].
  - kim2026programdistill: GPT-5.6 Sol builds the tasks [@kim2026programdistill, p. 2], GPT-6 Astra ranks first [@kim2026programdistill, p. 8], and GPT-6 Astra also classifies the failures [@kim2026programdistill, p. 12].
  - zhao2025vibe: Claude 4 Sonnet runs the environment-building agent [@zhao2025vibe, p. 17], and SWE-agent constructs the tasks [@zhao2025vibe, p. 4]. The best setting is SWE-agent + Claude 4 Sonnet [@zhao2025vibe, p. 7].
- **Overlap without a visible advantage** [V]:
  - liu2026benchmarking: GPT-4o built the annotations and is evaluated [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 13]; the best backbone is Claude-Haiku.
  - lu2025webgen: GPT-4o wrote the test cases and scored low [@lu2025webgen, p. 8].
  - bai2026recreationworld: the Qwen3.7-Plus judge is the lowest-scoring model (average 9.15) [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
  - chen2025iwr: the Gemini-2.5-Pro judge ranks mid-table [@chen2025iwr, p. 7].
  - wu2026looks: the judge is Gemini 2.5 Pro, Opus leads [@wu2026looks, p. 13], and the authors report no self-preference [A].
- [I] No paper tests construction-model or judge-model self-preference directly. The pattern is a validity threat, not a demonstrated bias.

## Agreements / converging evidence

- **G-A1. Whole-application functional fidelity is far from complete** [V]. Every benchmark agrees:
  - Full behavioural equivalence: 2.8% of apps [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11] and 0 of 200 programs [@yang2026programbench, p. 6].
  - Best workflow-level or requirement-level pass rates: 49–62% [@kim2026programdistill, p. 11; @liu2026benchmarking, p. 6; @tran2026vibe, p. 6].
  - Lower still in some benchmarks: IFS <25 [@chen2025iwr, p. 8], <45% [@pan2026functional, p. 5], 27.8% [@lu2025webgen, p. 8].
  - Strength [I]: **moderate**. The direction is consistent across 8 independent benchmarks, but 5 of them are preprints and most use single runs.
- **G-A2. Behaviour and interaction are harder than static structure** [V]:
  - Structure beats actions [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 16].
  - Static tasks score higher than interactive ones [@chen2025iwr, p. 16].
  - Interactive parts score lower than full pages [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 6].
  - UI plus logic is harder than logic alone [@kim2026programdistill, p. 38].
  - "Click has no effect" is the largest navigation failure category (48.4%) [@wu2026looks, p. 8].
  - Strength [I]: **moderate**, with the measurement caveat in C5.
- **G-A3. Fidelity falls as dependency depth, size or complexity rise** [V]: [@kim2026programdistill, p. 8; @yang2026programbench, p. 31; @tran2026vibe, p. 6; @zhao2025vibe, p. 14]. Strength [I]: **moderate**.
- **G-A4. Functional correctness and other quality dimensions diverge** [V]:
  - Best static quality but lowest Pass@1 [@molison2025llm, p. 8].
  - Correct but insecure [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6].
  - Equal functional scores but very different non-functional scores [@pan2026functional, p. 5].
  - The visual leader is not the maintainability leader [@wu2026looks, p. 7].
  - Authors state that passing functional tests does not imply maintainable code [A] [@tran2026vibe, p. 9].
  - Strength [I]: **moderate**. The pattern is consistent, but each study measures a different second dimension.
- **G-A5. Rebuilt code is structurally simpler and more monolithic than the original** [V]: [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9]. Strength [I]: **weak**. It rests on 2 preprints, selected subsets and size proxies only.
- **G-A6. Code quality and maintainability are rarely measured in fidelity benchmarks**:
  - Not measured at all [V]: [@si2025benchmarking, p. 3; @xiao2025benchmarking, p. 5; @kim2026programdistill, p. 14].
  - Explicitly left out [A]: [@tran2026vibe, p. 9].
  - Measured only by proxies [V]: size and structure [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9], LoC/reuse proxies [@wu2026looks, p. 4], a single MI index [@pan2026functional, p. 3], Likert ratings [@zhou2025declarui, p. 7].
  - Strength [I]: **strong** as a description of the field (verified absences across 12+ papers).
- **G-A7. LLM judges must be validated per judge model** [V]:
  - Judge–human agreement ranges from 36.1% to 86.4% depending on the evaluator model [@tran2026vibe, p. 9].
  - 86–94% raw agreement on 3 settings [@lu2025webgen, p. 9].
  - τ = 0.716 on 55 author-labelled scenarios [@wu2026looks, p. 13].
  - ρ = 0.65, tuned in-sample [@chen2025iwr, p. 17].
  - Low human inter-annotator κ (0.26–0.46) [@si2025benchmarking, p. 16].
  - Strength [I]: **moderate**.
- **G-A8. Practitioners perceive vibe-coded output as fast but flawed** [V]: [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 8]. This converges with LLM-linked code and design debt in mostly grey sources [@ehsani2026faster, p. 16] and with higher review burden for novice agent users [@asdaque2026novice, p. 3]. Strength [I]: **weak**. It rests on perception and proxy evidence, not code measurement.

## G3: It is unknown whether maintainability instruments agree with each other, and whether they predict maintenance effort, for AI-built applications

- Gap type: methodological / contradiction (C3, partly C1–C2).
- Evidence that the gap exists:
  - [A] PyExamine was chosen over SonarQube's "superficial linting" [@zhu2026understanding, p. 2]. [A] Technical-debt tools disagree on what counts as debt [@ehsani2026faster, p. 5]. [A] SonarQube and general linters are not designed for LLM-specific debt [@ehsani2026faster, p. 22], and LLM-aware quality tools are rarely independently evaluated [@ehsani2026faster, p. 28].
  - [A] SonarQube is called an "auxiliary indicator" only [@mota2026comparing, p. 6]. [V] borg2026echoes' outcome metric is a proprietary CodeHealth customised for the study, from the first author's employer [@borg2026echoes, p. 13; @borg2026echoes, p. 75].
  - [V] The direction of "LLM vs human" changes with the instrument and unit: fewer SonarQube bugs [@molison2025llm, p. 8], more repository warnings [@he2026speed, p. 7] that run mainly through code size [@he2026speed, p. 8], and smell counts that track LoC (ρ = 0.94) [@zhu2026understanding, p. 8].
  - [V] The only randomised maintenance outcome (second-developer time) showed no difference, while static measures in Phase 1 did show some [@borg2026echoes, p. 33; @borg2026echoes, p. 30]. The two kinds of measure were not related to each other.
- Novelty check (2026-11-12):
  - `rlab search` queries:
    1. "agreement between static analysis tools maintainability LLM-generated code" (openalex, arxiv; 2024)
    2. "SonarQube validity maintainability measurement developer perception AI-generated code" (crossref, openalex; 2023)
    3. "code smell detectors disagreement LLM generated code comparison of tools" (arxiv, openalex; 2024)
    4. "code quality maintainability of programs rebuilt by coding agents compared with original source" (arxiv, openalex; 2026)
  - WebSearch: "validity of SonarQube CodeHealth maintainability metrics for LLM-generated code agreement between tools human maintainability ratings 2026".
  - Closest prior work ([A], abstracts):
    - *Is Agent Code Less Maintainable Than Human Code?* (CodeThread; EMNLP 2026, DOI 10.18653/2026.emnlp-main.2528). Regression shows that "many traditional software engineering maintainability metrics do not explain" why agents do worse when building on agent code. The setting is issue-level repository patches with agents as maintainers. **This partly fills the original candidate**, so the gap is narrowed.
    - *Beyond Functional Correctness: Static Code Quality Profiling of LLM-Generated Code* (arXiv 2610.19167, preprint). Pylint, Radon and SonarQube on 65,663 LiveCodeBench programs. Single programs; the abstract mentions no tool-agreement or human validation.
    - *Comparing Open Source with Software Code Generated by AI Tools from Software Maintainability Quality Factor Perspective* (DOI 10.37394/232018.2025.13.58). MI, CC and Halstead on 3 tasks; no validation.
    - The WebSearch found no study that validates SonarQube or CodeHealth against human ratings or maintenance effort for LLM code.
  - Verdict: **partially novel (narrowed)**. Issue-level evidence that classic metrics fail to explain agent maintenance outcomes now exists (CodeThread). We found no study that, for whole AI-generated *applications*, (a) measures agreement among ≥3 maintainability instruments after size normalisation and (b) relates them to measured maintenance effort by humans or agents (searches on 2026-11-12).
- Confidence: **medium**. CodeThread and related 2026 work show the area is moving. Our claim is limited to application-level code and to inter-instrument agreement.
- Potential contribution: guidance on which (if any) static instruments a reconstruction study such as G1 should trust, and a test of the explanation offered for C1–C3.
- Suggested study / experiment:
  - Design: a measurement-validity (convergent and predictive validity) study.
  - Data: released generated full-stack apps from Vibe Code Bench [@tran2026vibe, p. 11]. Possibly also E2EDev outputs [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 9]. Sample about 60 apps across 4+ models.
  - Instruments: SonarQube (issues/KLoC, cognitive complexity), ESLint complexity rules, a Maintainability Index tool, jscpd duplication, and optionally CodeScene's free tier. All are normalised per KLoC or per function.
  - Criterion measures:
    1. Agent-maintainer success and cost on 2 scripted change requests per app (3 runs).
    2. Expert ranking by 3 raters of a 20-app subsample.
  - Analysis:
    - Kendall's W and pairwise Spearman correlations between instruments.
    - Mixed models predicting maintenance success from each instrument, controlling for size and functional pass rate.
    - Compare explained variance between instruments.
  - Threats to validity:
    - Agent-maintainer success depends on the maintainer model.
    - Apps from different models differ in features, not only in quality (control with functional pass rate).
    - Rater expertise.
- Feasibility for a beginner: **easy–moderate**. Existing released apps, free tools and scripted change tasks. The statistics are standard.

    - *Trajectory-Level Security Debt in LLM Coding Agents* (DOI 10.1609/aaaiss.v10i1.43533). SAST on ProgramBench rebuilds. Security only, with no comparison to the originals (see `reports/novelty-check-security-fidelity.md` §3).
    - *Software Aging in LLM-Generated Applications* (arXiv 2608.26391, preprint). Runtime aging of spec-generated BaxBench back-ends. Not reconstruction.
    - *SWE-CI* (arXiv 2603.03823, preprint). Maintainability as the change in functional correctness over long CI histories. Not reconstruction.
  - Verdict: **novel** for the narrow claim. We found no study that rebuilds existing applications from observable artefacts (UI, screenshots, behaviour) and then measures, on the same rebuilds, (a) behavioural fidelity against the original and (b) maintainability with more than one size-normalised instrument plus a maintenance task, using the original as the baseline (searches on 2026-11-12). Measuring each part separately is not new.
- Confidence: **medium-high**. The evidence is strong and consistent across the corpus. Novelty rests on abstract-level reading of eight close 2026 papers, mostly preprints, and the field publishes monthly. Re-run the check before submission.
- Potential contribution: the first reference-anchored "fidelity × maintainability" profile of AI reconstruction. It would show whether rebuilds that behave like the original are also as easy to change as the original. It would also test whether the size reduction [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15] means simpler code or missing functionality, which C8 in the evidence matrix leaves open.
- Suggested study / experiment:
  - Design: a within-app factorial benchmark study, apps × tools × repeated runs.
  - Data and sample:
    - 8–10 small web apps (about 1–5 KLoC, React or plain JS, with a back-end of at most simple CRUD).
    - Stratum A (5 apps): public apps from the released E2EDev set, which come with validated BDD tests [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 5; @liu2026benchmarking, p. 9].
    - Stratum B (3–5 apps): apps first published after the evaluated models' training cutoffs, or apps the researcher writes. This also gives a contamination contrast (G5).
  - Builder input: the running original (URL) plus screenshots only. No source code, no `data-testid` hints.
  - Arms: 2–3 builders (e.g. one terminal coding agent and one commercial vibe-coding platform). Record tool versions and dates. Run each builder 3 times per app, which gives about 60–90 rebuilds.
  - Fidelity metrics:
    1. Pass rate of Playwright/BDD tests written against the original with role- and text-based locators. Each test must pass on the original (100%) before use.
    2. A secondary visual score.
  - Maintainability metrics, each also computed on the original, with the rebuild/original ratio as the outcome:
    1. SonarQube issues per KLoC and cognitive complexity per function.
    2. Duplication % (SonarQube) plus a second analyser (ESLint complexity rules or a Maintainability Index tool).
    3. A standard change task: 2 small feature changes, each with its own acceptance tests. The task is done by a fixed "maintainer" agent (3 runs) on the original and on each rebuild; outcomes are success and tokens/time, following the CodeThread idea. An optional pilot with 4–6 student developers follows the hand-off design of borg2026echoes [@borg2026echoes, p. 13].
  - Baseline: the original app on every measure.
  - Analysis:
    - Preregister the hypotheses.
    - Mixed-effects models with app as a random effect.
    - Report mean ± SD over runs with bootstrap CIs.
    - Report the Spearman correlation between fidelity and the maintainability ratio across rebuilds.
    - Normalise all counts by size; this matters because of C8 and [@he2026speed, p. 8].
  - Expected threats to validity:
    - Small app sample (external validity).
    - Tool drift between runs (record versions; run all arms in the same week).
    - Finite test suites give only a lower bound on fidelity [@yang2026programbench, p. 12; @bai2026recreationworld, p. 22].
    - Static instruments are not validated for AI code (G3).
    - The agent-as-maintainer confounds AI capability with code maintainability.
    - Contamination in Stratum A.
- Feasibility for a beginner: **moderate**. All tools are free or have free tiers, and E2EDev provides apps and tests. The main effort is writing locator-independent tests for Stratum B and managing about 60–90 rebuilds. API cost is moderate. This needs supervision on the statistics.

## Is Vibe Coding Safe? Benchmarking Vulnerability of Agent-Generated Code in Real-World Tasks

> **Takeaway:** Code that passes its functional tests is often not secure. Even the best AI coding agent produced working code for 57.0% of tasks, but only 11.8% of tasks were solved both correctly and securely, so "it works" and "it is good code" must be measured separately.

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Authors | Songwen Zhao, Danqing Wang, Kexun Zhang, Jiaxuan Luo, Zhuo Li, Lei Li |
| Year · Venue | 2025 · Published at ICML 2026 (our copy: arXiv v4) |
| Status | Peer-reviewed (ICML 2026, PMLR 306, per the PDF footer; our metadata still lists it as an arXiv preprint) |
| Identifier | arXiv 2512.03262 (DOI 10.48550/arxiv.2512.03262) |
| Paper type | Benchmark plus comparative evaluation of AI coding agents |
| Relevance to us | Medium — RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5 |

### In plain words
"Vibe coding" means asking an AI agent in plain language to build a feature, and then using the result with little human checking. This paper asks a simple question: is the code that such agents write safe to put into real software? The authors built a test set of 186 real programming tasks where human programmers had once written code with a security hole. They then asked 12 different AI agent setups to write the same features and checked two things: does the code work, and is it secure? The answer is worrying: most working solutions still contain the old security hole. This matters for us because it shows that checking whether software "behaves correctly" says little about other qualities of the code.

### How they did it
1. They started from real security fixes in open-source Python projects. Each fix has a "before" version (with the vulnerability) and an "after" version (fixed) [V] [@zhao2025vibe, p. 3].
2. In the "before" version, an AI agent removed (masked) the code of one feature. A second agent wrote a feature request in the style of a GitHub issue (a short task description). The description had to explain what the feature does, without any hint about security [V] [@zhao2025vibe, p. 4; @zhao2025vibe, p. 16].
3. The masks were built on the vulnerable version, not the fixed one, so that no information from the fix leaks into the task [A] [@zhao2025vibe, p. 4].
4. Each AI agent then had to re-implement the missing feature inside the full repository. It could run code and use the results, for up to 200 steps [V] [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6].
5. Two kinds of tests were run on the result. Functional tests (the project's existing tests) check whether the feature works. Security tests (tests added by the historical fix) check whether the old vulnerability is back [V] [@zhao2025vibe, p. 4; @zhao2025vibe, p. 5].
6. Scoring used pass@1 (the share of tasks solved on the first and only try). FuncPass counts tasks that pass the functional tests; SecPass counts tasks that pass both functional and security tests [V] [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6]. No AI judge was used for scoring [V] [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6].
7. Five software-engineering experts checked the security tests and rewrote those that were too tied to one specific implementation [V] [@zhao2025vibe, p. 19].

### Data and setup
- 186 tasks from 100 Python repositories, covering 10 application domains and 79 CWE types (CWE = a standard catalogue of software weakness types) [V] [@zhao2025vibe, p. 2; @zhao2025vibe, p. 13].
- Tasks are large: on average 236K lines of context, a 175.0-line target change, 66.9 functional tests and 3.5 security tests per task [V] [@zhao2025vibe, p. 5].
- 12 agent settings: 3 agent frameworks (SWE-agent, OpenHands, Claude Code) times 4 models (Claude 4 Sonnet, Kimi K2, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 3 Pro) [V] [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6].
- One run per task. Temperature, exact model versions and cost are not reported [V] [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6].
- The main runs already include a short generic security reminder in the prompt [V] [@zhao2025vibe, p. 7].

### Key findings
- [V] The best setting, SWE-agent with Claude 4 Sonnet, reached FuncPass 57.0% but SecPass only 11.8% [@zhao2025vibe, p. 7]. 79.3% of its working solutions were insecure [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6].
- [V] Across all 12 settings, FuncPass ranged from 12.9% to 57.0% and SecPass from 3.8% to 12.9% [@zhao2025vibe, p. 7].
- [V] Success drops when the change spans more files. For Claude 4 Sonnet, FuncPass fell from 66.9% (one file) to 30.3% (more than two files), and SecPass from 15.4% to 3.0% [@zhao2025vibe, p. 14].
- [V] Simple security prompting helped little. Giving the agent the exact weakness type raised SecPass from 11.8% to 15.1%, while FuncPass fell from 57.0% to 55.4%; letting the agent pick weakness types itself gave 50.0% / 14.5% [@zhao2025vibe, p. 8].
- [V] When asked to choose weakness types, agents picked 7.2 types per task against 1.1 true types, with precision of only 0.086 to 0.114 [@zhao2025vibe, p. 9].
- [V] On tasks that all models solved, Gemini 2.5 Pro had the highest secure share (30.4% vs 18.3% for Claude 4 Sonnet), although it was functionally the weakest [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6]. [I] Treat this ranking as weak: the size of this shared subset is never reported and can be at most about 24 to 37 tasks per framework, based on the FuncPass numbers [@zhao2025vibe, p. 7].

### Limitations and weaknesses
- [A] Python only; tests are a practical stand-in for security, and the tests may not cover all weaknesses [@zhao2025vibe, p. 24].
- [A] Security tests from historical fixes can reject secure alternative solutions; 6.5% were tied to the original implementation and were rewritten [@zhao2025vibe, p. 19].
- [I] Only one run per task and no confidence intervals. With 186 tasks, one task is about 0.54 percentage points, so small differences such as 11.8% vs 12.9% may be noise [@zhao2025vibe, p. 7].
- [I] No agreement score between the five experts is reported [@zhao2025vibe, p. 19].
- [I] The tasks rebuild public historical code from popular projects, so models may have seen the fixed versions in training; the paper does not discuss this [@zhao2025vibe, p. 13].
- [I] Claude 4 Sonnet built the test environments [@zhao2025vibe, p. 17] and SWE-agent built the tasks [@zhao2025vibe, p. 4], and SWE-agent with Claude 4 Sonnet scored best. A "home advantage" is possible but untested.
- [I] Only the known historical vulnerability is tested (3.5 tests per task), so other new holes go unseen; SecPass is an upper bound on "secure" [@zhao2025vibe, p. 5].

### Gaps and future work this paper leaves open
- [A] The authors call for more languages, property-based and adversarial tests, static analysis and security-aware training [@zhao2025vibe, p. 24].
- [I] It measures security, not maintainability, and patches, not whole applications. This is part of G1 (fidelity and maintainability of rebuilt apps are never measured together).
- [I] The possible builder–winner overlap is one of the cases behind G2 (same-family bias between benchmark builder and evaluated model).
- [I] Its coupled security tests are an example for G7 (tests tied to the original's code can unfairly fail valid rebuilds).
- [I] Training-data exposure of public repositories is not addressed, which links to G5.

### Why it matters for your research
This paper is your clearest evidence that "it passes the tests" and "it is good code" are different things [I]. Its task design is worth reusing: hide an existing implementation, describe it in words, let an AI rebuild it, then test it against the original's own tests. That is close to a reconstruction study. Reuse the idea of two separate scores (one for behaviour, one for a quality dimension). They then asked 12 different AI agent setups to write the same features and checked two things: does the code work, and is it secure? The answer is worrying: most working solutions still contain the old security hole. 1. They started from real security fixes in open-source Python projects. Each fix has a "before" version (with the vulnerability) and an "after" version (fixed) [V] [@zhao2025vibe, p. 3].
2. In the "before" version, an AI agent removed (masked) the code of one feature. A second agent wrote a feature request in the style of a GitHub issue (a short task description). The description had to explain what the feature does, without any hint about security [V] [@zhao2025vibe, p. 4; @zhao2025vibe, p. 16].
3. The masks were built on the vulnerable version, not the fixed one, so that no information from the fix leaks into the task [A] [@zhao2025vibe, p. 4].
4. Each AI agent then had to re-implement the missing feature inside the full repository. It could run code and use the results, for up to 200 steps [V] [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6].
5. Two kinds of tests were run on the result. Functional tests (the project's existing tests) check whether the feature works. Security tests (tests added by the historical fix) check whether the old vulnerability is back [V] [@zhao2025vibe, p. 4; @zhao2025vibe, p. 5].
6. Scoring used pass@1 (the share of tasks solved on the first and only try). FuncPass counts tasks that pass the functional tests; SecPass counts tasks that pass both functional and security tests [V] [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6]. No AI judge was used for scoring [V] [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6].
7. Five software-engineering experts checked the security tests and rewrote those that were too tied to one specific implementation [V] [@zhao2025vibe, p. 19].

- 186 tasks from 100 Python repositories, covering 10 application domains and 79 CWE types (CWE = a standard catalogue of software weakness types) [V] [@zhao2025vibe, p. 2; @zhao2025vibe, p. 13].

## PropGen: Automated Property Generation for Property-Based Testing of Mobile Apps

> **Takeaway:** An AI model can write down valid behaviour rules of an Android app by actually using the app, but not from the app's description alone (912 of 985 rules valid vs 0 of 240). For us, this is a method for turning an original app's observed behaviour into tests a rebuild must pass [@xiong2026propgen, p. 8; @xiong2026propgen, p. 9].

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Authors | Yiheng Xiong, Shiwen Song, Bo Ma, Ting Su, Xiaofei Xie |
| Year · Venue | 2026 · Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026) |
| Status | Peer-reviewed |
| Identifier | DOI 10.1145/3832783.3837536 (arXiv 2604.13463) |
| Paper type | Tool paper with empirical evaluation |
| Relevance to us | Medium — RQ2, RQ4, RQ5 (method only; not RQ3) |

### In plain words
Many app bugs do not crash the app. The app just does the wrong thing, for example a setting that has no effect. Such bugs are hard to find because there is no "oracle" (a rule that says what the correct result is). Property-based testing helps: you write rules like "if I delete a note, it is no longer in the list", and a tool tries many random action sequences to see if a rule is broken. Writing those rules by hand is slow and expensive, and apps rarely have written specifications [A] [@xiong2026propgen, p. 1]. PropGen lets an AI model explore a running Android app, record what it sees, and turn that evidence into such rules automatically.

### How they did it
1. Exploration. A multimodal LLM (an AI model that reads both images and text) looks at the screenshot, the numbered on-screen widgets, the app name and the screen (activity) names from the app's manifest file. It guesses which functions the app has, and PropGen tries each guess step by step [V] [@xiong2026propgen, p. 4].
2. Evidence. Each tried action is saved as "behavioural evidence": the screen before, the action, the screen after, what changed, and whether it worked [V] [@xiong2026propgen, p. 5].
3. Grounding. Widget names are filtered against a list of text strings taken from the app package by static analysis (reading the files without running them) [V] [@xiong2026propgen, p. 5]. [I] So PropGen is grey-box: it mostly watches the running app, but also reads the manifest and a string list. The authors describe it as exploring "a black-box app" [A] [@xiong2026propgen, p. 11].
4. Property writing. The model first writes a rule in plain language with three parts: precondition (when it applies), interaction (what the user does) and postcondition (what must be true after). It then turns the rule into code for the testing tool Kea [V] [@xiong2026propgen, p. 6].
5. Refinement. When a human confirms that a reported "bug" is a false alarm, the model finds which of the three parts is wrong and fixes only that part [V] [@xiong2026propgen, p. 6].

### Data and setup
- 12 open-source Android apps (for example OmniNotes, Markor, AnkiDroid, NewPipe), from 57,529 to 403,785 lines of code [V] [@xiong2026propgen, p. 7].
- Model: GPT-5.2 (snapshot gpt-5.2-2025-12-11) at temperature 1.0. 3 hours per app for exploration and rule writing, then 6 hours of testing [V] [@xiong2026propgen, p. 7].
- Comparisons: DroidAgent (another AI exploration tool), a naive baseline where the LLM writes 20 rules per app from the app's description only, and four bug-finding tools (Genie, Odin, PBFDroid, VisionDroid) [V] [@xiong2026propgen, p. 7].
- Two graduate students, not co-authors, judged validity independently. Their agreement was high: Cohen's kappa (an agreement score where 1 is perfect) of 0.91, 0.82 and 0.81 [V] [@xiong2026propgen, p. 7].
- No repeated runs are reported [I] [@xiong2026propgen, p. 8].

### Key findings
- [V] PropGen found 1,282 app functions, of which 1,210 were valid (94.4%) and 977 were executed correctly (76.2%). DroidAgent found 575, with 491 valid (85.4%) and 187 correctly executed (32.5%) [@xiong2026propgen, p. 8].
- [V] PropGen wrote 985 rules, and 912 were valid (92.6%; 78.7% to 98.8% per app) [@xiong2026propgen, p. 8].
- [V] The naive baseline that only read the app description wrote 240 rules, and none were valid, because it referred to widgets that do not exist [@xiong2026propgen, p. 9].
- [V] 127 rules caused false alarms; 118 of them (92.9%) were fixed, mostly by changing the postcondition (64) or precondition (53) [@xiong2026propgen, p. 9].
- [V] The rules found 25 previously unknown functional bugs; 5 were fixed by developers at the time of writing [@xiong2026propgen, p. 9].
- [V] Only 3 of the 25 bugs were found again by the four older tools. Those tools found 13 unknown bugs themselves, of which PropGen missed 10 [@xiong2026propgen, p. 10]. [A] The authors call the approaches "complementary rather than substitutable" [@xiong2026propgen, p. 10].
- [V] Cost was about $14.86 per app for PropGen vs $13.01 for DroidAgent [@xiong2026propgen, p. 9].

### Limitations and weaknesses
- [A] Human judging can be subjective; only 12 apps were tested; the open-source apps may be in the model's training data [@xiong2026propgen, p. 11].
- [A] The model sometimes invents functions that do not exist or invents widgets while writing rules [@xiong2026propgen, p. 9].
- [I] Not fully automatic: refinement starts only after a human confirms a false alarm, and that human effort is not measured [@xiong2026propgen, p. 6].
- [I] Single runs at temperature 1.0, so we do not know how stable the numbers are [@xiong2026propgen, p. 7].
- [I] The naive baseline never sees the app, so it is a weak comparison [@xiong2026propgen, p. 7].
- [I] Three of the four comparison tools (Genie, Odin, PBFDroid) come from the authors' own research group, and the scope check was validated by the same group [@xiong2026propgen, p. 8]. Only VisionDroid is independent.
- [I] The contamination check is partial: showing that the bugs were not previously reported does not show that the model never saw how the apps behave [@xiong2026propgen, p. 11].

### Gaps and future work this paper leaves open
- [A] The authors plan a larger and broader set of apps, better step planning, and combining PropGen with other test oracles [@xiong2026propgen, p. 10; @xiong2026propgen, p. 11].
- [I] Nobody has used properties mined from an original app to test an AI-rebuilt version of it. This would serve the fidelity side of G1.
- [I] Mobile apps and their hidden back-end behaviour are barely studied in reconstruction (G8); PropGen's runtime exploration could help there.
- [I] Testing six app builds released after the model's training cutoff [A] [@xiong2026propgen, p. 11] is one of the few contamination controls in our corpus, relevant to G5.
- [I] Its rules use on-screen behaviour rather than the original's internal identifiers, which is relevant to G7.

### Why it matters for your research
PropGen does not build or rebuild apps, so it says nothing about code quality [I]. Its value is as a method. It shows how to recover what an app does from the running app, without source code or a specification. You could use the same idea to write tests from your original app and then check how many of them the rebuild satisfies. Its strongest lesson: an AI that has not observed the real app invents behaviour, so ground any test or rebuild in observed behaviour [V] [@xiong2026propgen, p. 9]. Its evaluation design, with two independent annotators and a kappa score, is a good template.

### Connections to other papers
- [V] Like bai2026recreationworld, which uses accessibility and DOM tests [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 9], it checks behaviour on the running app rather than in the code.
- [V] Its post-cutoff app builds are one of the few explicit contamination controls, next to yang2026programbench's no-internet setup and ablation [@yang2026programbench, p. 6].
- [V] Its finding that a description-only LLM invents widgets fits zhou2025declarui, which needed a page-transition graph and refinement loop for good navigation coverage [@zhou2025declarui, p. 10].
- [I] It differs from kim2026programdistill, whose oracles use the original's selectors [@kim2026programdistill, p. 35]; PropGen's rules are grounded in visible widgets and text.

## Is LLM-Generated Code More Maintainable & Reliable Than Human-Written Code?

> **Takeaway:** GPT-4o code had far fewer SonarQube-flagged "bugs" than human competition code, but it was often functionally wrong, and the fine-tuned model with the best quality scores had the lowest correctness. Static quality and correctness must be measured together, and the "fewer bugs" headline rests on a weak human baseline [@molison2025llm, p. 8].

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Authors | Alfred Santa Molison, Marcia Moraes, Glaucia Melo, Fabio Santos, Wesley K. G. Assunção |
| Year · Venue | 2025 · ACM/IEEE International Symposium on Empirical Software Engineering and Measurement (ESEM 2025) |
| Status | Peer-reviewed (our copy: arXiv v1, page numbers refer to it) |
| Identifier | DOI 10.1109/esem64174.2025.00036 (arXiv 2508.00700) |
| Paper type | Quantitative comparative study (static analysis) |
| Relevance to us | Medium — RQ3 (main), RQ2, RQ4, RQ5 |

### In plain words
People worry that AI-written code is harder to maintain than human code. This paper compares Python code written by GPT-4o with code written by humans for the same programming puzzles. It uses SonarQube, a widely used tool that scans code without running it and flags problems. The authors look at "bugs" (rule-based warnings about likely errors), "code smells" (signs of messy or hard-to-change code) and the estimated time to fix them. They also run a small check of whether the code actually gives the right answers. The study matters because it is one of the few peer-reviewed, direct AI-versus-human quality comparisons in our set.

### How they did it
1. They took coding puzzles from the APPS dataset, a public set of 10,000 Python problems at three difficulty levels (introductory, interview, competition), with human solutions from sites such as Codeforces [V] [@molison2025llm, p. 3].
2. GPT-4o (version 2024-08-06) wrote solutions in three ways [V] [@molison2025llm, p. 4]:
3. Zero-shot: just the problem and the instruction to solve it.
4. Few-shot: the problem plus all human solutions to that same problem as examples.
5. Fine-tuned: a GPT-4o model trained on 240 question–answer pairs (80 per level), tested on 480 questions (160 per level).
6. All solutions were scanned with SonarQube using its default Python rules [V] [@molison2025llm, p. 4; @molison2025llm, p. 5].
7. They compared groups with odds ratios (how much more or less likely a problem is in one group than another) and, for fix time, a Mann-Whitney U test with Cliff's delta (an effect-size measure) [V] [@molison2025llm, p. 5].
8. Three authors ran 15 solutions per approach (5 per level) by hand to compute Pass@1 (share of solutions that pass the tests on the first try) [V] [@molison2025llm, p. 8].

### Data and setup
- Dataset: APPS, Python, three difficulty levels [V] [@molison2025llm, p. 3].
- Model: GPT-4o-2024-08-06, temperature 1.00, max 2,048 tokens [V] [@molison2025llm, p. 4].
- Number of human and zero-/few-shot solutions actually scanned: not reported [I] [@molison2025llm, p. 4].
- Tool: SonarQube Free Server edition, default quality profile [V] [@molison2025llm, p. 4].
- Correctness check: 15 solutions per approach [V] [@molison2025llm, p. 8].
- Replication package on Zenodo [V] [@molison2025llm, p. 11].

### Key findings
- [V] SonarQube found no security vulnerabilities in any group [@molison2025llm, p. 5].
- [V] The odds of a SonarQube bug in GPT-4o code vs human code were tiny in every setting and level (odds ratios 0.00 to 0.019, all p < 0.001) [@molison2025llm, p. 8]. [I] The 0.00 means one group had no bugs at all, so it is not a real estimate.
- [V] Code smells were mixed: zero-shot code had 3.57 times the odds of a smell on introductory problems, while fine-tuned code had fewer smells; several comparisons were not significant [@molison2025llm, p. 8].
- [V] Estimated fix effort was lower for AI code on easy tasks but not on competition tasks (human 6.95 min, few-shot 7.33, fine-tuned 7.60) [@molison2025llm, p. 7].
- [V] Pass@1 was 1.0 for humans, 0.87 few-shot, 0.53 zero-shot and 0.47 fine-tuned [@molison2025llm, p. 8].
- [A] The fine-tuned model has "the best quality metrics" yet struggled with complex solutions [@molison2025llm, p. 8].
- [A] On competition-level problems, AI code may carry more critical-severity issues than human code [@molison2025llm, p. 6].

### Limitations and weaknesses
- [A] Python only, puzzle-style tasks, one model, and possible prompt sensitivity [@molison2025llm, p. 10].
- [A] SonarQube may not capture all aspects of quality, and its fix-time estimates may not match real developer effort [@molison2025llm, p. 10].
- [I] Leakage: the few-shot prompt contains the human solutions it is compared against, so few-shot vs human is not an independent comparison [@molison2025llm, p. 4].
- [I] A SonarQube "bug" is a rule-based warning, not a failing program. Quality was also measured on solutions that fail the tests, so "fewer bugs" does not mean "more correct" [@molison2025llm, p. 8].
- [I] The human baseline is competition code written to be correct, not maintainable, as the authors admit [@molison2025llm, p. 9].
- [I] Group sizes are not reported, there are no confidence intervals and no correction for many comparisons, and the Pass@1 check uses only 15 solutions per approach [@molison2025llm, p. 8].
- [I] APPS has been public since 2021, so GPT-4o may have seen it in training; this is not discussed [@molison2025llm, p. 11].
- [I] Some numbers are inconsistent, for example few-shot Pass@1 is 0.86 in the introduction and 0.87 in the table [@molison2025llm, p. 1; @molison2025llm, p. 8].

### Gaps and future work this paper leaves open
- [A] The authors suggest other LLMs, more languages and quality metrics, retrieval-augmented generation and cost–quality trade-off studies [@molison2025llm, p. 10].
- [I] It studies single small programs, not applications, and has no original app to compare against. This is the core of G1.
- [I] Its "fewer bugs" result conflicts in direction with studies that use other units or tools. Whether quality tools agree, and whether they predict real maintenance effort, is G3.
- [I] Public benchmark data and possible training exposure link to G5.

### Why it matters for your research
This paper gives you a ready-made recipe for the code-quality part of a study: SonarQube default profile, bugs, smells, severity and fix effort [I]. It also gives a strong warning. The model with the best quality scores was the least correct, so always report quality and correctness side by side, ideally quality only for code that works. Avoid its design mistakes: do not show the baseline to the model, report group sizes, use a realistic human baseline, and run several samples per task.

### Connections to other papers
- [V] Agrees with zhao2025vibe that correctness and another quality dimension diverge: there, 79.3% of working solutions failed security tests [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6].
- [V] Seems to disagree with he2026speed, where adopting Cursor raised repository SonarQube warnings by 30.26% [@he2026speed, p. 7]. [I] The units differ (single puzzle solutions vs whole repositories over months), so neither result refutes the other.
- [A] zhu2026understanding chose a different tool (PyExamine) to avoid SonarQube's "superficial linting" [@zhu2026understanding, p. 2] and found more Long Method smells in larger models' code than in human code [@zhu2026understanding, p. 7].
- [V] zhu2026understanding also builds on this paper: its zero-shot prompt replicates Santa et al. [@zhu2026understanding, p. 4].

3. Zero-shot: just the problem and the instruction to solve it.
4. Few-shot: the problem plus all human solutions to that same problem as examples.
5. Fine-tuned: a GPT-4o model trained on 240 question–answer pairs (80 per level), tested on 480 questions (160 per level).
6. All solutions were scanned with SonarQube using its default Python rules [V] [@molison2025llm, p. 4; @molison2025llm, p. 5].
7. They compared groups with odds ratios (how much more or less likely a problem is in one group than another) and, for fix time, a Mann-Whitney U test with Cliff's delta (an effect-size measure) [V] [@molison2025llm, p. 5].
8. Three authors ran 15 solutions per approach (5 per level) by hand to compute Pass@1 (share of solutions that pass the tests on the first try) [V] [@molison2025llm, p. 8].

- Experiment I: 90 problems, 5 models, 2 prompts, plus 90 human solutions; one Python file per solution [V] [@zhu2026understanding, p. 4].

- Temperature, model hosting and the PyExamine version are not reported [I] [@zhu2026understanding, p. 4].
- Functional correctness of the generated code was not measured [I] [@zhu2026understanding, p. 9].

- 9 web apps, 3 per platform: Lovable, v0 and Replit, generated 6–21 May 2026 on free tiers [V] [@mota2026comparing, p. 2].

**Corrections I applied:**
- **zhao2025vibe:** the venue reads "Published at ICML 2026 (our copy: arXiv v4)". I checked the ICML/PMLR 306 footer on p. 1. The "Gemini 2.5 Pro most secure" result is labelled weak because the subset it rests on is unreported and at most about 24–37 tasks per framework.

**Status and uncertain points:**
1. **zhu2026understanding:** marked peer-reviewed at ASE 2026, but our PDF is the arXiv v1 preprint with a different title. The link between that PDF and the DOI is probable, not confirmed; the brief says so in its Status row.
2. **mota2026comparing:** marked as a preprint. Its page header names SBES 2026, but the artefact link is "anonymized for review" and no acceptance is stated.
3. **Experiment II in zhu2026understanding:** the sample of about 20 apps is our estimate from the reported p-values; the paper does not state it. The brief labels this [I].
4. **Connection between molison2025llm and zhu2026understanding:** this one is not in the analyses or the evidence matrix. I confirmed it in the zhu full text: it mirrors molison's design (p. 3) and criticises its SonarQube-based conclusions (p. 2), citing it as reference [17].

**Left out for lack of support:**
- A connection between xiong2026propgen and zhou2025declarui, which I had first drafted. No project file links them.
- Mota's "fast but flawed" match: I first wrote it as if Mota uses that phrase. I rewrote it to cite Mota's own wording (p. 5) next to the quote from fawzy2026vibe (p. 8).
- For zhu2026understanding, I removed the citation to a page for "functional correctness not measured". It is now an [I] statement based on our check of all pages.

I did not update STATUS.md or run `rlab log`, because you asked me to write no other files.
